weeks.title: FAR U1·W1 — Conceptual Framework & the Four Statements (CPA Core · from CMA m1)
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — build every statement from one illustrative trial balance

Fictionalized case facts: the MBG general ledger totals $12,480,000.00 and Riverton totals $16,920,000.00, both balanced. FAR begins where the CMA program began (month 1): the trial balance is the anchor, and every financial statement is derived from it. This CPA Core unit teaches the conceptual framework and the four statements at exam depth, using MBG's illustrative ledger as the worked example.

The FASB conceptual framework

The objective of general-purpose financial reporting is to provide information useful to investors, lenders, and creditors in making decisions about providing resources. Two fundamental qualitative characteristics make information useful: relevance (it can influence decisions — predictive value, confirmatory value, materiality) and faithful representation (complete, neutral, and free from error). Four enhancing characteristics improve usefulness: comparability, verifiability, timeliness, and understandability. The overriding constraint is cost versus benefit.

The framework also defines the elements (assets, liabilities, equity, revenues, expenses, gains, losses), the assumptions (economic entity, going concern, monetary unit, periodicity), and the principles (historical cost, revenue recognition, matching, full disclosure). For MBG, the economic-entity assumption is why MBG and Riverton are never combined on a single statement — each is its own reporting entity.

The four statements and how they articulate

  • Balance sheet (statement of financial position) — assets = liabilities + equity at a point in time. MBG's WIP/construction-in-progress sits here as an asset until a home closes.
  • Income statement — revenues − expenses = net income for a period.
  • Statement of changes in equity — beginning equity + net income + contributions − distributions = ending equity.
  • Statement of cash flows — operating, investing, and financing cash flows reconciling beginning to ending cash.

Articulation ties them together: net income from the income statement flows into the statement of changes in equity, whose ending equity appears on the balance sheet, and the change in cash on the balance sheet equals the bottom line of the cash flow statement. A set of statements that does not articulate is internally inconsistent — the same discipline as keeping MBG's trial balance in balance.

Worked articulation on MBG

Illustrative figures anchored to MBG's scale: beginning equity $4,000,000, net income $988,000 (from the CMA program's illustrative income statement), and owner distributions $300,000. Ending equity = $4,000,000 + $988,000 − $300,000 = $4,688,000, which is the equity figure that must appear on the period-end balance sheet. If the balance sheet showed a different equity number, the statements would not articulate and an error exists to find — exactly the reconciliation mindset the construction close demands.

Recognition and measurement bases

FAR tests multiple measurement bases: historical cost, net realizable value, current/replacement cost, present value, and fair value (ASC 820, introduced in CMA month 7). An item is recognized when it meets an element definition and is measurable. Knowing which basis applies to which account — receivables at net realizable value, most PP&E at historical cost less depreciation, certain investments at fair value — is a recurring FAR exam skill.

The elements and the five measurement attributes

The framework defines ten elements: assets, liabilities, and equity (the balance-sheet elements), revenues, expenses, gains, and losses (the income elements), plus investments by owners, distributions to owners, and comprehensive income. Precise definitions matter on the exam: an asset is a present right to an economic benefit the entity controls as a result of a past event; a liability is a present obligation to transfer an economic benefit. The difference between revenues/expenses (from ongoing major operations) and gains/losses (from peripheral or incidental transactions) drives where an item is presented and whether it is shown gross or net.

FAR also tests five measurement attributes and which applies to which account: historical cost (most PP&E and inventory at acquisition), current/replacement cost, net realizable value (receivables, and inventory under the lower-of-cost-or-NRV rule), present value of future cash flows (long-term receivables and payables, leases, pensions), and fair value (many financial instruments). The mixed-attribute model means a single balance sheet carries accounts measured several different ways, which is itself a frequent exam point.

Comprehensive income and the accrual basis

Comprehensive income is the change in equity from non-owner sources, and it equals net income plus other comprehensive income (OCI). OCI collects specific items the standards route around the income statement until realized: unrealized gains/losses on available-for-sale debt securities, the effective portion of cash-flow hedges, foreign-currency translation adjustments, and certain pension adjustments. Memorizing the OCI population is high-yield, because the recurring trap is whether an item hits net income now or waits in OCI.

Financial statements are prepared on the accrual basis: revenue is recognized when earned and expenses when incurred, independent of cash timing — the discipline that lets a construction contractor recognize revenue as work is performed rather than when paid. The going-concern assumption underlies the historical-cost model; if substantial doubt about continuing as a going concern exists, management must evaluate and disclose it, and severe cases shift measurement toward liquidation values.

Notes and the full-disclosure principle

The statements are incomplete without the notes. The full-disclosure principle requires the summary of significant accounting policies, the detail behind summarized line items, and disclosure of risks, commitments, contingencies, and subsequent events. A user cannot assess a contractor's position from the face of the balance sheet alone — backlog, surety commitments, related-party transactions, and the revenue-recognition method all live in the notes. The framework, the elements, the measurement attributes, and the disclosure principle together define what a faithful, decision-useful set of statements must contain — the foundation every later FAR topic builds on.

Where US GAAP and IFRS diverge

The CPA exam expects awareness of key IFRS contrasts even though it tests US GAAP primarily. Both frameworks share the same objective and qualitative characteristics, but they differ in application: IFRS permits a revaluation model for PP&E and intangibles (carrying assets at fair value), allows reversal of most impairment losses, prohibits LIFO for inventory, and uses a single control-based model for consolidation. US GAAP is more rules-based in places, prohibits PP&E revaluation, and bars reversal of impairments on assets held for use. Knowing where the two diverge prevents applying an IFRS rule on a US-GAAP question and vice versa. The conceptual framework, in the end, is not abstract theory — it is the source of the recognition, measurement, presentation, and disclosure rules the remaining FAR units apply transaction by transaction, and it is the anchor an examiner returns to whenever a fact pattern has no single obvious specific rule.

CMA bridge

This unit is the FAR counterpart to CMA month 1 (External Financial Reporting). The CMA program taught you to build statements from MBG's illustrative trial balance; FAR adds the authoritative framework, the qualitative characteristics, and the standards-level rigor the CPA exam expects.

Practice and recap

  1. State the objective of financial reporting and the two fundamental qualitative characteristics.
  2. List the four statements and how net income, equity, and cash articulate across them.
  3. Compute ending equity and tie it to the balance sheet.
  4. Match an account to its measurement basis.

Recap: the conceptual framework makes relevance and faithful representation the test of useful information; the four statements articulate so net income, equity, and cash all tie; and MBG's illustrative ending equity of $4,688,000 must reconcile across the set — the trial-balance discipline carried into FAR.

weeks.title: FAR U1·W2 — Revenue Recognition Under ASC 606 (CPA Core · from CMA m1/m4)
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — when does a half-built house earn revenue?

A construction contract is the textbook ASC 606 problem, and MBG lives it on every job. Revenue is not recognized when cash is collected or when the home closes — it is recognized as the performance obligation is satisfied over time, measured by progress. This is the same percentage-of-completion logic the CMA WIP schedule (month 4) used; FAR adds the authoritative five-step model.

The five-step model

  1. Identify the contract with a customer (approval, rights, payment terms, commercial substance, collectibility probable).
  2. Identify the performance obligations — distinct goods or services promised.
  3. Determine the transaction price, including variable consideration (change orders, incentives, penalties) constrained to amounts highly probable not to reverse.
  4. Allocate the transaction price to the performance obligations based on relative standalone selling prices.
  5. Recognize revenue when (point in time) or as (over time) each obligation is satisfied.

Over time versus a point in time

Revenue is recognized over time if any one criterion is met: the customer simultaneously receives and consumes the benefits; the entity creates or enhances an asset the customer controls; or the asset has no alternative use and the entity has an enforceable right to payment for work completed. A typical construction contract on the customer's land meets the over-time criteria. If none are met, revenue is recognized at a point in time (e.g., a spec home sold from inventory recognizes at closing when control transfers).

Measuring progress — cost-to-cost

For over-time recognition, progress is measured by an input or output method; construction commonly uses the cost-to-cost input method: percent complete = costs incurred to date ÷ total estimated costs. Illustrative contract: price $2,000,000, total estimated cost $1,600,000, costs incurred to date $800,000.

Percent complete = $800,000 ÷ $1,600,000 = 50%. Cumulative revenue = 50% × $2,000,000 = $1,000,000; cost of revenue $800,000; gross profit $200,000.

Contract assets and contract liabilities

Compare revenue recognized to amounts billed. With billings to date of $900,000 against recognized revenue of $1,000,000, the entity has under-billed by $100,000 — a contract asset (costs and estimated earnings in excess of billings) of $100,000. If instead billings were $1,150,000, the entity would have a contract liability (billings in excess of costs) of $150,000. This is exactly the over/under-billing schedule from CMA month 4 — FAR names the balance-sheet accounts contract asset and contract liability.

Estimate changes and losses

Changes in estimated cost or price are accounted for prospectively as a change in estimate — catch up the cumulative percent-complete in the current period, not by restating prior periods. But an expected loss on a contract is recognized immediately and in full as soon as it is anticipated, regardless of percent complete — the conservatism the CMA gross-profit-fade discussion warned about.

Transaction price, variable consideration, and the constraint

Step three — determining the transaction price — is where construction contracts get hard, because the price includes variable consideration: change orders, claims, performance bonuses, and liquidated-damages penalties. The entity estimates variable consideration using either the expected value (probability-weighted) or the most likely amount, whichever better predicts the outcome. Crucially, the estimate is subject to the constraint: include variable consideration only to the extent it is highly probable that a significant revenue reversal will not occur. An unapproved change order is therefore not booked at its full hoped-for value; it is constrained until approval makes the amount highly probable. The transaction price also reflects a significant financing component when payment timing gives one party a material financing benefit, and any noncash consideration is measured at fair value.

Contract modifications follow their own rules. A modification is treated as a separate contract if it adds distinct goods/services at their standalone price; otherwise it is accounted for prospectively (a termination-and-new-contract) or through a cumulative catch-up, depending on whether the remaining goods are distinct. Change orders on a single, integrated construction job typically fold into the existing performance obligation with a cumulative catch-up to percent-complete.

Principal versus agent, contract costs, and licenses

When another party is involved, the entity decides whether it is a principal (it controls the good/service before transfer — record revenue gross) or an agent (it arranges for another to provide it — record only the net commission). A general contractor that controls and is responsible for subcontracted work is generally a principal and reports the gross contract revenue, not just its markup.

ASC 340-40 governs contract costs: the incremental costs of obtaining a contract (a sales commission paid only on winning) are capitalized and amortized if recovery is expected, while costs of obtaining a contract that would have been incurred regardless are expensed. Costs to fulfill a contract are capitalized only if they relate directly to the contract, generate or enhance resources used to satisfy it, and are expected to be recovered. Finally, revenue from licenses of intellectual property is recognized either over time (a right to access IP that changes over the license period) or at a point in time (a right to use IP as it exists at grant) — a distinction the exam tests alongside the over-time-versus-point-in-time criteria for goods and services.

Presentation, disclosure, and the contract balances

ASC 606 also dictates presentation. Netting a contract's rights and obligations produces either a contract asset (revenue recognized ahead of the unconditional right to bill) or a contract liability (consideration received or due ahead of performance), shown separately from an unconditional receivable — a right to payment conditioned only on the passage of time. The distinction matters because a receivable is subject to credit-loss measurement while a contract asset carries both performance and credit risk, and a single contract is presented net rather than grossed up.

The standard's disclosure requirements are extensive: disaggregation of revenue into categories that depict how economic factors affect it; the opening and closing contract balances and the revenue recognized from prior-period contract liabilities; the remaining performance obligations (backlog) and when they will be recognized; and the significant judgments in applying the five steps, including how variable consideration and the constraint were estimated. For a contractor these disclosures surface the backlog and change-order judgments the face of the statements cannot show, which is exactly why a sophisticated reader looks to the notes first and why ASC 606 is as much a disclosure standard as a recognition one. The recognition and the disclosure travel together: a revenue number the notes cannot explain — with what judgments, against what backlog, under what constraint — is an incomplete answer to the question the standard was written to address.

CMA bridge

CMA month 4 built the WIP schedule and over/under-billings operationally; FAR formalizes it as ASC 606 with the five steps, the over-time criteria, and the contract-asset/contract-liability terminology. The $100,000 underbilling here is the same figure as the CMA flagship exemplar.

Practice and recap

  1. Apply the five steps in order.
  2. Test the three over-time criteria; otherwise recognize at a point in time.
  3. Measure progress with cost-to-cost and compute cumulative revenue.
  4. Classify under-billing as a contract asset and over-billing as a contract liability.
  5. Treat estimate changes prospectively but recognize anticipated losses immediately.

Recap: ASC 606's five steps recognize a construction contract's revenue over time by cost-to-cost; at 50% complete MBG's illustrative contract shows $1,000,000 revenue and a $100,000 contract asset — the WIP schedule from CMA month 4 expressed in FAR's language.

weeks.title: FAR U1·W3 — PP&E: Capitalization, Depreciation & Impairment (CPA Core · from CMA m4/m11)
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — what goes into the cost of MBG's excavator?

Property, plant, and equipment is a heavily tested FAR area and a daily MBG decision: what is capitalized, how it is depreciated, and when it is written down. The CMA program treated the depreciation tax shield (month 11) as a cash flow; FAR governs the financial-accounting measurement underneath it.

Capitalization — what is included in cost

The cost of an asset includes its purchase price plus all costs necessary to get it ready for its intended use: freight-in, installation, testing, sales tax, and (for self-constructed assets) directly attributable labor, materials, and overhead. Avoidable interest on borrowings during the construction of a qualifying asset is capitalized (interest capitalization), not expensed. After acquisition, repairs and maintenance are expensed while betterments that increase capacity, efficiency, or useful life are capitalized.

Depreciation methods

Depreciation allocates depreciable cost (cost − salvage) over the useful life. Illustrative: equipment cost $440,000, salvage $40,000, life 5 years.

  • Straight-line = (cost − salvage) ÷ life = ($440,000 − $40,000) ÷ 5 = $80,000 per year.
  • Double-declining-balance applies twice the straight-line rate (2 ÷ 5 = 40%) to the beginning book value, ignoring salvage until book value nears it: year 1 = 40% × $440,000 = $176,000.
  • Units-of-production allocates by output; sum-of-the-years'-digits is another accelerated method.

Accelerated methods front-load expense (and, in tax, the deduction and its shield), but total depreciation over the life is identical across methods.

Impairment of long-lived assets (ASC 360)

Test a long-lived asset for impairment when indicators exist (declining use, market value drop, adverse changes). The two-step test:

  1. Recoverability: if carrying value exceeds the undiscounted future cash flows, the asset is impaired.
  2. Measurement: impairment loss = carrying value − fair value.

Illustrative: equipment with a carrying value of $300,000 has undiscounted future cash flows of $260,000. Because $300,000 > $260,000, it is impaired. If fair value is $220,000, the impairment loss = $300,000 − $220,000 = $80,000. Note the test uses undiscounted cash flows but the loss is measured to fair value — a classic exam trap. Under US GAAP, impairment losses on assets held for use are not reversed.

Disposals

On disposal, the gain or loss = proceeds − book value (cost − accumulated depreciation). Record depreciation up to the disposal date first. For an asset classified as held for sale, stop depreciating and measure at the lower of carrying value or fair value less costs to sell.

Capitalized interest, exchanges, and depletion

When an entity constructs an asset for its own use over time, it capitalizes interest on the funds tied up during construction — the avoidable interest, computed on the weighted-average accumulated expenditures, capped at the actual interest incurred for the period. Interest capitalization stops when the asset is substantially complete and ready for use. Nonmonetary exchanges of assets are recorded at fair value (recognizing the full gain or loss) when the exchange has commercial substance — that is, when the future cash flows change as a result; lacking commercial substance, the asset received is recorded at the book value of the asset given up and gains are generally deferred. Natural resources are subject to depletion, typically on a units-of-production basis over the estimated recoverable reserves.

A further obligation, the asset retirement obligation (ARO), arises when law or contract requires the entity to dismantle or restore at the end of an asset's life. The ARO is recognized at the present value of the expected retirement cost, added to the asset's carrying amount, and accreted to its future value over time while the capitalized cost depreciates — a pairing the exam likes to test.

Intangibles, goodwill, and held-for-sale

Intangible assets with finite lives are amortized over their useful lives and tested for impairment like other long-lived assets; those with indefinite lives (and goodwill) are not amortized but are tested for impairment at least annually. Goodwill impairment under current guidance is a one-step test at the reporting-unit level: if the unit's carrying amount exceeds its fair value, the impairment loss equals that excess, limited to the goodwill balance — the older two-step measurement was eliminated. Internally generated goodwill and most internally generated intangibles are not capitalized; research and development is generally expensed as incurred (with specific exceptions for certain software and acquired in-process items).

An asset (or disposal group) is classified as held for sale when management commits to a plan, the asset is available for immediate sale, and the sale is probable within a year. On classification, the entity stops depreciating it and measures it at the lower of carrying amount or fair value less costs to sell — and, unlike held-for-use impairments, a subsequent recovery in fair value can be recognized up to the previously recognized loss. Together these rules round out the life cycle of long-lived assets from capitalization through use, impairment, and disposal.

Componentization, costs after acquisition, and the IFRS contrast

Two refinements recur. First, costs incurred after acquisition are capitalized only if they extend the asset's useful life, increase its capacity, or improve its efficiency (a betterment); ordinary repairs and maintenance that merely keep the asset operating are expensed. Distinguishing a capital improvement from a repair is a frequent exam judgment with a real cash-and-earnings consequence. Second, under IFRS, significant components of an asset with different useful lives must be depreciated separately (component depreciation) — a roof and the building shell, for instance — whereas US GAAP permits but does not require it.

The IFRS contrast extends to measurement: IFRS allows the revaluation model, carrying PP&E at fair value with increases generally to a revaluation surplus in OCI, and permits reversal of a prior impairment if the asset's value recovers — both prohibited under US GAAP for assets held for use. IFRS also tests impairment in a single step by comparing carrying amount to the higher of fair-value-less-costs-to-sell and value-in-use, using discounted cash flows, where US GAAP's recoverability test uses undiscounted cash flows. Holding these differences straight is the difference between a right and a wrong answer when a question signals which framework applies. In short, US GAAP tests recoverability against undiscounted cash flows and forbids both revaluation and impairment reversal for assets held for use, while IFRS discounts, permits revaluation to a surplus in OCI, and allows reversal — a compact set of contrasts that recurs across the entire FAR blueprint, not only in long-lived assets, and one worth committing to memory as a single block.

CMA bridge

CMA month 11 used straight-line depreciation to compute the tax shield ($80,000 × tax rate); FAR is where the depreciation expense itself, the capitalization rules, and impairment are measured. The numbers tie: the same $80,000 straight-line figure appears in both.

Practice and recap

  1. Capitalize purchase price plus costs to ready the asset; expense repairs, capitalize betterments.
  2. Compute straight-line and double-declining-balance depreciation.
  3. Apply the two-step impairment test: undiscounted cash flows for recoverability, fair value for measurement.
  4. Compute gain/loss on disposal as proceeds minus book value.

Recap: PP&E is recorded at full cost-to-ready, depreciated by a chosen method ($80,000 straight-line or $176,000 first-year double-declining), and written down when carrying value exceeds undiscounted cash flows — with the $80,000 illustrative impairment measured to fair value.

weeks.title: FAR U1·W4 — Leases (ASC 842) & Contingencies (ASC 450) (CPA Core · from CMA m7/m10)
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — the leased equipment is now on the balance sheet

CMA month 7 flagged that ASC 842 brought operating leases onto the balance sheet. FAR is where that is measured. MBG leases vehicles and equipment, and under ASC 842 a lessee recognizes a right-of-use (ROU) asset and a lease liability for essentially every lease over twelve months. This week measures leases and then covers loss contingencies — warranty, litigation, and bond-claim accruals.

Lessee accounting under ASC 842

At commencement, the lessee records a lease liability at the present value of the remaining lease payments, discounted at the rate implicit in the lease (or the incremental borrowing rate if that is not determinable), and an ROU asset equal to the liability plus initial direct costs and prepayments, less incentives. Both finance and operating leases are on the balance sheet; the difference is the expense pattern.

Worked measurement

Illustrative: five annual payments of $50,000 at an 8% discount rate. The ordinary-annuity present-value factor (8%, 5 years) is 3.9927, so the lease liability = $50,000 × 3.9927 = $199,635, and the ROU asset begins at the same amount (absent initial direct costs).

Finance versus operating classification

A lease is a finance lease (lessee) if any one criterion is met: ownership transfers at the end; a purchase option is reasonably certain to be exercised; the lease term is a major part of the asset's remaining life; the present value of payments is substantially all of the asset's fair value; or the asset is so specialized it has no alternative use to the lessor. Otherwise it is an operating lease.

The expense pattern differs: a finance lease records amortization of the ROU asset plus interest on the liability — front-loaded total expense. An operating lease records a single straight-line lease expense. Both reduce the same lease liability as payments are made.

Loss contingencies (ASC 450)

A loss contingency is accounted for by likelihood:

  • Probable and reasonably estimable → accrue a liability and recognize the loss (if a range, accrue the best estimate, or the minimum of the range when no amount is better).
  • Reasonably possible (or probable but not estimable) → disclose only.
  • Remote → generally ignore (no accrual, no disclosure).

For MBG, a probable, estimable warranty obligation or an adverse, estimable litigation outcome is accrued; a merely possible performance-bond claim is disclosed. Gain contingencies are not accrued (to avoid recognizing income before realization); they may be disclosed if probable.

Lessor accounting and the lease mechanics

The lessee's mirror image is the lessor, who classifies a lease as sales-type, direct-financing, or operating. A sales-type lease (the lessee gains control — the same five criteria) lets the lessor derecognize the asset and recognize a net investment in the lease plus any selling profit at commencement. A direct-financing lease arises when no sales-type criterion is met but two conditions both hold: (a) the present value of the lease payments plus any qualifying residual-value guarantee equals substantially all of the asset's fair value, and (b) collection of the lease payments plus any amount needed to satisfy a residual-value guarantee is probable. The residual guarantee does not itself make collection probable; it is a separate input to the PV test. In a direct-financing lease the selling profit is deferred into interest income over the term. An operating lease keeps the asset on the lessor's books and recognizes lease income straight-line. The exam tests matching the lessee and lessor sides of the same lease.

Two practical points round out the lessee mechanics. A short-term lease (12 months or less, with no purchase option reasonably certain) may be exempted from balance-sheet recognition and expensed straight-line — a policy election by class of asset. Lease payments included in the liability are fixed payments, in-substance fixed payments, variable payments tied to an index/rate (at the initial rate), reasonably-certain purchase-option and penalty amounts, and amounts probable under residual-value guarantees; payments that are purely usage- or sales-based are excluded and expensed as incurred. The ROU asset is subsequently measured differently for finance leases (amortized separately) versus operating leases (a single straight-line cost that backs into the ROU amortization).

Worked contingency accruals and subsequent events

Return to contingencies with two worked cases. A warranty: if MBG estimates that 2% of a completed project's $5,000,000 value will require warranty work, the obligation is probable and estimable, so it accrues a $100,000 warranty liability with a matching expense in the period of sale. A lawsuit: counsel assesses a probable loss in a range of $200,000 to $500,000 with no amount better than another — the entity accrues the minimum, $200,000, and discloses the range up to $500,000. If the same suit were only reasonably possible, it would be disclosed but not accrued; if remote, neither.

Finally, subsequent events interact with contingencies. A recognized (Type I) subsequent event provides evidence about conditions existing at the balance-sheet date — a lawsuit settled before issuance for a then-existing claim adjusts the accrual. A non-recognized (Type II) event reflects new conditions arising after the date — a fire or a new lawsuit filed after year-end — and is disclosed but not accrued. Distinguishing the two, like distinguishing accrue-versus-disclose, is exactly the judgment FAR rewards.

Sale-leaseback and the disclosure picture

A sale-leaseback — selling an asset and immediately leasing it back — is tested for whether a sale actually occurred under ASC 606's control criteria. If control transfers, the seller-lessee recognizes the sale (and any gain, adjusted for off-market terms) and records a lease for the right retained; if control does not transfer (for example, a leaseback that is effectively a finance lease, or a repurchase option that retains control), no sale is recognized and the transaction is accounted for as a financing. This prevents a contractor from manufacturing a gain by selling and leasing back equipment it never really gave up.

Lease accounting also carries its own disclosures: the components of lease cost, weighted-average remaining lease term and discount rate, and a maturity analysis of lease liabilities, plus qualitative information about leasing arrangements. Combined with the contingency and subsequent-event judgments, the picture this week completes is that the balance sheet now reflects obligations — leases and accrued contingencies — that an older model left in the footnotes, and that the notes still carry the commitments, guarantees, and post-date events a reader needs to assess the entity's true position. Recognizing what belongs on the face versus in the notes, and accruing versus disclosing, is the core competence FAR is testing across leases and contingencies alike. Master that line — face versus notes, accrue versus disclose, and sale versus financing — and the unit's hardest fact patterns resolve into a small number of repeatable decisions.

CMA bridge

CMA month 7 (week 4) introduced ASC 842 at a conceptual level and month 10 covered risk; FAR measures the lease liability and ROU asset and sets the accrual rules for the warranty and litigation contingencies that risk management identifies. The threads connect: identify the risk in CMA, measure and disclose it in FAR.

Practice and recap

  1. Recognize an ROU asset and lease liability at the present value of lease payments for leases over twelve months.
  2. Classify finance vs operating by the five criteria; know the expense patterns differ.
  3. Accrue a loss contingency that is probable and estimable; disclose if reasonably possible; ignore if remote.
  4. Do not accrue gain contingencies.

Recap: ASC 842 puts the $199,635 lease liability and ROU asset on MBG's balance sheet; finance leases front-load expense while operating leases are straight-line; and loss contingencies are accrued only when probable and estimable, with gain contingencies never accrued.

weeks.title: FAR U2·W1 — Investments: Debt & Equity Securities, Equity Method (CPA Core)
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — where does the gain go?

The single most-tested idea in FAR investments is where an unrealized gain lands — net income or other comprehensive income — and that depends entirely on classification. The same $15,000 gain hits earnings under one classification and bypasses earnings under another. This unit sorts debt securities, equity securities, and significant-influence investments.

Debt securities — three classifications

  • Held-to-maturity (HTM) — intent and ability to hold to maturity. Reported at amortized cost; unrealized changes are not recognized.
  • Trading — bought to sell short-term. Reported at fair value with unrealized gains/losses in net income.
  • Available-for-sale (AFS) — the default for debt not in the other two. Reported at fair value with unrealized gains/losses in other comprehensive income (OCI) until sold.

Illustrative: a debt security cost $100,000 and is worth $115,000 at year-end. As trading, the $15,000 unrealized gain goes to net income. As AFS, the same $15,000 goes to OCI. As HTM, no gain is recognized — it stays at amortized cost.

Equity securities

For equity investments without significant influence, the rule is simpler: report at fair value with changes in net income (there is no AFS treatment for equity securities under current GAAP). So an equity security held at fair value runs its unrealized gains and losses through earnings each period. A narrow practicability exception lets an entity measure an equity security without a readily determinable fair value at cost less impairment, adjusted for observable price changes.

Significant influence — the equity method

When an investor owns roughly 20% to 50% of the voting stock (presumed significant influence), it uses the equity method, not fair value. The investment is recorded at cost and then:

  • increased by the investor's share of investee net income (and decreased by its share of losses), and
  • decreased by dividends received (dividends are a return of investment, not income).

Illustrative: buy 30% for $300,000. The investee earns $200,000 → add 30% × $200,000 = $60,000 to the investment and to equity-method income. The investee pays $50,000 of dividends → reduce the investment by 30% × $50,000 = $15,000. Ending investment = $300,000 + $60,000 − $15,000 = $345,000. Above 50% ownership, the investor consolidates instead (the intercompany-elimination logic from CMA month 7).

Impairment and credit losses

HTM debt securities follow the CECL model (ASC 326): the investor records an allowance for expected credit losses through net income and presents the security net of that allowance, recognizing expected losses up front rather than waiting for a loss event. AFS debt securities use a separate model: when fair value is below amortized cost and the shortfall is credit-related, the investor recognizes an allowance for credit losses in net income — capped at the difference between fair value and amortized cost — while any non-credit portion of the decline stays in OCI. If the entity intends to sell, or will more likely than not be required to sell before recovery, it writes the security all the way down to fair value through earnings. Equity securities need no OCI-impairment model because their changes already run through net income; the lone exception is the practicability-election equity security carried at cost, which is assessed qualitatively and written down to fair value through earnings when impaired.

Selling a security and the reclassification adjustment

When an AFS debt security is sold, the cumulative unrealized gain or loss sitting in accumulated OCI is removed and the realized gain or loss recognized in net income — a reclassification adjustment. If the AFS security that rose to $115,000 is later sold, the amount previously parked in OCI is reclassified out of OCI and into earnings so comprehensive income is not double-counted. Trading securities need no such adjustment because their gains already hit earnings each period. This OCI-recycling mechanic is a favorite trap: an AFS gain is recognized in earnings only when realized, while the periodic mark waits in OCI in the interim.

Reclassifications between categories

Transfers among HTM, AFS, and trading are recorded at fair value on the transfer date, and the unrealized gain’s treatment depends on direction. Transferring into trading recognizes the unrealized gain immediately in net income; transferring out of trading leaves the already-recognized gain in income. Moving debt from HTM to AFS books the unrealized gain in OCI; from AFS to HTM, the existing OCI amount is amortized over the remaining life. Frequent sales or transfers out of HTM can taint the whole HTM portfolio and force reclassification to AFS — which is why HTM demands genuine positive intent and ability to hold to maturity.

Equity-method nuances the exam tests

Beyond add-income / subtract-dividends, the equity method carries subtleties. At acquisition, any excess of cost over the investor’s share of the investee’s book value is a basis difference allocated to identifiable assets (then depreciated or amortized against equity-method income), with the remainder treated as equity-method goodwill (not amortized). The investor also eliminates its share of intra-entity profits on transactions with the investee until realized. If the investee reports losses, the investor records its share only down to a zero investment balance (plus any loans or guarantees), then suspends further losses until the investee returns to profit. An investor may instead elect the fair value option — an irrevocable, instrument-by-instrument choice — carrying the investment at fair value through earnings.

Worked basis difference: pay $300,000 for 30% when 30% of book value is $250,000. Of the $50,000 excess, say $30,000 relates to undervalued equipment with a 10-year life and $20,000 is goodwill. The investor amortizes $3,000 per year ($30,000 ÷ 10) against equity-method income while leaving the $20,000 goodwill intact — so first-year equity income of $60,000 becomes $57,000 after the basis-difference amortization.

A worked AFS year in journal entries

Trace one AFS debt security through a full cycle. Buy at $100,000: debit AFS investment $100,000, credit cash. At year-end fair value $115,000: debit the fair-value adjustment $15,000 and credit unrealized gain — OCI $15,000, so the balance sheet shows $115,000 with $15,000 in accumulated OCI. Next year fair value slips to $108,000 before sale: debit unrealized holding loss — OCI $7,000, credit the adjustment $7,000, leaving $8,000 in accumulated OCI. On sale at $108,000: derecognize the carrying amount, remove the $8,000 accumulated OCI, and recognize a realized gain in net income equal to proceeds minus original cost ($108,000 − $100,000 = $8,000). The cumulative effect on comprehensive income over the holding period equals the single $8,000 economic gain — OCI merely timed it.

IFRS contrast

IFRS 9 classifies financial assets by a business-model test and a cash-flow characteristics (SPPI) test rather than by management-intent labels. Debt instruments fall into amortized cost (held to collect contractual cash flows that are solely principal and interest), fair value through OCI (held to collect and sell), or fair value through profit or loss (everything else). For equity investments not held for trading, IFRS permits an irrevocable election to present fair-value changes in OCI — but, unlike US GAAP debt-AFS, those amounts are never recycled to profit or loss on sale. IFRS applies a single expected-credit-loss model across debt instruments, whereas US GAAP splits CECL (HTM) from the AFS allowance approach. The equity method exists under both frameworks at significant influence.

CMA bridge

CMA month 7 covered fair value (ASC 820) and intercompany eliminations; FAR investments add the classification rules that decide whether a fair-value change hits net income or OCI, and the equity method that bridges between fair-value accounting and full consolidation.

Practice and recap

  1. Classify a debt security as HTM (amortized cost), trading (FV → NI), or AFS (FV → OCI).
  2. Carry equity securities at fair value through net income (no AFS for equity).
  3. Apply the equity method at 20–50%: add share of income, subtract dividends.
  4. Consolidate above 50%.

Recap: classification decides the destination — a $15,000 unrealized gain is net income if trading, OCI if AFS, and unrecognized if HTM. At 30% ownership the equity method carries the investment to $345,000 after adding $60,000 of income and subtracting $15,000 of dividends.

weeks.title: FAR U2·W2 — Accounting for Income Taxes (ASC 740) (CPA Core · from CMA m11)
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — book income and taxable income are not the same number

MBG depreciates equipment one way for the books and a faster way for taxes (the CMA month 11 tax shield). That difference does not vanish — it creates a deferred tax. ASC 740 reconciles the financial statements to the tax return by recognizing the future tax consequences of today's differences. This is consistently one of FAR's hardest and most-tested areas.

Income tax expense has two parts

Total income tax expense = current tax expense + deferred tax expense. Current is the tax actually payable on this year's taxable income. Deferred is the change in deferred tax assets and liabilities arising from temporary differences that will reverse in future periods.

Temporary versus permanent differences

Temporary differences arise when an item hits the books and the tax return in different periods; they reverse over time and create deferred taxes:

  • A taxable temporary difference (taxable later) creates a deferred tax liability (DTL) — e.g., tax depreciation exceeding book depreciation now.
  • A deductible temporary difference (deductible later) creates a deferred tax asset (DTA) — e.g., a warranty accrued for books but deducted for tax only when paid, or unearned revenue taxed when received.

Permanent differences never reverse and create no deferred tax — they only change the effective tax rate. Examples: tax-exempt municipal bond interest, fines and penalties, and the nondeductible portion of certain expenses.

Worked deferred tax

Illustrative, tying to Unit 1: in year 1, book (straight-line) depreciation is $80,000 while tax depreciation is $176,000. Tax depreciation exceeds book by $96,000 — a taxable temporary difference. At an enacted future rate of 24%, the deferred tax liability = $96,000 × 24% = $23,040. In later years book depreciation will exceed tax depreciation and the DTL reverses back toward zero. Deferred taxes are always measured at the enacted rate expected when the difference reverses — not the current rate if a change is already enacted.

Valuation allowance

A deferred tax asset is recognized in full, then reduced by a valuation allowance if it is more likely than not (greater than 50% probability) that some portion will not be realized — for instance, if future taxable income may be insufficient to use a deductible difference or a net operating loss carryforward. The allowance is a contra-asset that lowers the net DTA, and it is reassessed each period.

Net operating losses

When deductions exceed income, the result is a net operating loss (NOL). Under current US rules an NOL generally cannot be carried back and is carried forward indefinitely, but its use in any future year is limited to 80% of that year’s taxable income. An NOL carryforward is a deductible item that creates a deferred tax asset, subject to the same valuation-allowance test: if it is more likely than not that future taxable income will be insufficient to absorb the carryforward, a valuation allowance reduces the DTA. The exam often pairs a fresh NOL with a weak earnings history to test whether the allowance is required.

Enacted rate changes and intraperiod allocation

Deferred taxes use the enacted rate for the period of expected reversal. When a new rate is enacted, every existing DTA and DTL is remeasured at the new rate in the period of enactment, and the adjustment runs through income tax expense from continuing operations — even when the underlying difference originated in OCI. Separately, intraperiod tax allocation spreads the total provision across the statements: tax is allocated to continuing operations first, then to discontinued operations and to items recognized directly in OCI (such as AFS and pension gains), so each component is presented net of its own tax effect.

Uncertain tax positions

ASC 740 prescribes a two-step approach for uncertain tax positions. Step 1 — recognition: a benefit is recognized only if the position is more likely than not to be sustained on its technical merits, assuming the authority has full information. Step 2 — measurement: the benefit recognized is the largest amount greater than 50% likely to be realized on settlement, using a cumulative-probability table. If a $100,000 deduction has a 60% cumulative probability of yielding at least a $60,000 benefit, the entity recognizes $60,000 and records a liability for the unrecognized $40,000. Interest and penalties on the unrecognized portion are accrued per the entity’s policy.

Balance-sheet classification and the rate reconciliation

All deferred tax assets and liabilities are classified as noncurrent, and DTAs and DTLs within the same tax jurisdiction are netted to a single noncurrent amount. Public companies disclose a rate reconciliation bridging the statutory rate to the effective tax rate — the line where permanent differences do their work. Tax-exempt municipal interest pushes the effective rate below statutory; nondeductible fines and penalties push it above. Because permanent differences never create deferred taxes, they enter the provision only through the current computation and the ETR reconciliation, never on the deferred side.

Worked provision and IFRS contrast

Worked provision: pretax book income is $500,000, including $20,000 of tax-exempt municipal interest (permanent) and the $96,000 excess tax depreciation (temporary). Taxable income = $500,000 − $20,000 − $96,000 = $384,000; at 24% the current tax payable is $92,160. The temporary difference adds deferred tax expense of $96,000 × 24% = $23,040 (the DTL). Total tax expense = $92,160 + $23,040 = $115,200 — an effective rate of 23.04% on book income, below statutory 24% precisely because the municipal interest is permanently excluded.

IFRS contrast: IAS 12 reaches deferred taxes through a similar temporary-difference model but differs in two tested ways. It uses no valuation allowance — a DTA is recognized only to the extent it is probable that future taxable profit will be available (a net presentation, not a contra-account). And it measures deferred taxes at the rate that is enacted or substantively enacted, a slightly broader trigger than US GAAP’s strict enacted-only rule. Both frameworks classify all deferred taxes as noncurrent.

A worked deferred tax asset

Mirror the DTL with a deductible difference. Suppose MBG accrues a $40,000 warranty liability for the books but cannot deduct it for tax until the work is performed. The expense reduces book income now but not taxable income, so taxable income exceeds book income this year and a deferred tax asset of $40,000 × 24% = $9,600 is recognized — the future tax saving when the warranty is paid and deducted. If management judges it more likely than not that only $30,000 of the underlying deduction will ultimately be usable, a valuation allowance trims the net DTA to $30,000 × 24% = $7,200. Netting this DTA against the period’s DTL yields the single noncurrent deferred tax balance reported within the jurisdiction.

CMA bridge

CMA month 11 used the depreciation tax shield as a cash flow; FAR explains the financial-statement counterpart — the deferred tax liability the faster tax depreciation creates. The $96,000 book-versus-tax gap there is the temporary difference here.

Practice and recap

  1. Split tax expense into current and deferred.
  2. Classify a difference as temporary (creates deferred tax) or permanent (no deferred tax).
  3. Tax depreciation > book → DTL; warranty/unearned revenue → DTA.
  4. Measure deferred taxes at the enacted future rate; reduce a DTA by a valuation allowance when more likely than not unrealizable.

Recap: ASC 740 recognizes the future tax effects of temporary differences — the $96,000 excess of tax over book depreciation creates a $23,040 deferred tax liability at 24% — while permanent differences only move the effective rate and a valuation allowance trims a DTA that is more likely than not unrealizable.

flashcards.back: No; they never reverse and only change the effective tax rate.

weeks.title: FAR U2·W3 — Stockholders' Equity & Earnings Per Share (CPA Core)
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — the bottom line per share

Equity transactions and earnings per share are FAR staples. Even a closely held builder must understand par, additional paid-in capital, treasury stock, dividends, and — for any entity with public reporting aspirations — the EPS computation. This unit covers the equity accounts and the basic/diluted EPS calculation.

The equity accounts

Contributed capital splits into par (or stated) value of stock issued and additional paid-in capital (APIC) — the excess over par. Retained earnings accumulates net income less dividends. Treasury stock (reacquired shares) and accumulated other comprehensive income complete the section. Issuing stock for more than par debits cash, credits common stock at par, and credits APIC for the excess.

Treasury stock — cost method

Under the common cost method, reacquiring shares debits Treasury stock at the repurchase cost (a contra-equity account). Reissuing above cost credits APIC — treasury stock; reissuing below cost debits APIC — treasury (to the extent available) and then retained earnings. Treasury stock is not an asset and never produces a gain or loss in net income — equity transactions with owners do not touch the income statement.

Dividends and splits

  • Cash dividend: a liability is recorded at declaration (debit retained earnings, credit dividends payable); paid later. There is no entry on the record date.
  • Small stock dividend (less than 20–25%): capitalize retained earnings at fair value of the shares issued.
  • Large stock dividend (more than 20–25%): capitalize at par value.
  • Property dividend: remeasure the asset to fair value (recognizing a gain/loss), then distribute at fair value.
  • Stock split: no journal entry — par per share falls and share count rises proportionally.

Earnings per share

Basic EPS = (net income − preferred dividends) ÷ weighted-average common shares outstanding. Preferred dividends are subtracted because EPS measures earnings available to common shareholders.

Illustrative: net income $988,000, preferred dividends $88,000, weighted-average common shares 300,000. Basic EPS = ($988,000 − $88,000) ÷ 300,000 = $900,000 ÷ 300,000 = $3.00.

Diluted EPS adjusts for dilutive potential common shares — stock options (via the treasury-stock method) and convertible securities (via the if-converted method). Only securities that reduce EPS are included; antidilutive securities are excluded. Diluted EPS is therefore always less than or equal to basic EPS.

Treasury stock — the par-value method

An alternative to the cost method is the par-value method, which treats reacquisition as a constructive retirement. On repurchase, Treasury stock is debited at par, the original APIC tied to those shares is removed proportionally, and any remaining difference is debited to retained earnings (or credited to APIC from retirement). Presentation differs too: under the par method treasury stock is deducted from common stock at par, whereas under the cost method the single treasury-stock figure is deducted from total equity. Both methods agree on the bedrock rule — no gain or loss on a company’s dealings in its own shares ever reaches net income.

Preferred stock and dividends in arrears

Preferred stock features drive both equity presentation and the EPS numerator. Cumulative preferred accumulates unpaid dividends as dividends in arrears — not a liability until declared, but disclosed and paid before common dividends. Participating preferred shares in dividends beyond its stated rate; convertible preferred can be exchanged for common (relevant to diluted EPS); callable preferred can be reacquired by the issuer. For basic EPS, subtract the current-year dividend on cumulative preferred whether or not declared; for noncumulative preferred, subtract only dividends actually declared. That declared-versus-cumulative distinction is a classic EPS trap.

The weighted-average share count

Basic EPS divides by the weighted-average number of common shares, time-weighting each block by the fraction of the year it was outstanding. Shares issued for cash are weighted from the issuance date; treasury shares repurchased are removed from that date forward. Stock dividends and splits are treated retroactively — applied to all periods presented as if they existed from the beginning, because they change the share count without changing resources. Worked count: 280,000 shares outstanding on January 1, issue 60,000 on April 1, and repurchase 24,000 treasury shares on October 1. Weighted average = 280,000 + (60,000 × 9/12) − (24,000 × 3/12) = 280,000 + 45,000 − 6,000 = 319,000 shares.

Diluted EPS — the two mechanics worked

Treasury-stock method (options/warrants): assume in-the-money options are exercised and the proceeds buy back shares at the average market price; the net increase in shares joins the denominator. If 30,000 options with a $20 exercise price exist while the average market price is $25, exercise brings in $600,000, which repurchases 24,000 shares ($600,000 ÷ $25), so 6,000 net new shares are added. If-converted method (convertible bonds/preferred): assume conversion at the later of issuance or period start; add the convertible’s shares to the denominator and add back the after-tax interest (for bonds) or the preferred dividend (for preferred) to the numerator. Each security is tested individually and included only if it lowers EPS; an antidilutive security — one that would raise EPS — is excluded, and securities are considered from most to least dilutive so a later antidilutive one cannot mask an earlier dilutive effect.

Retained earnings events and IFRS contrast

Several events route through equity rather than income. A prior-period adjustment — correcting an error in previously issued statements — is recorded net of tax against the opening balance of retained earnings, not in current income. An appropriation of retained earnings earmarks a portion as unavailable for dividends but remains part of equity; it creates no asset and no expense. Under IFRS (IAS 33), basic and diluted EPS are computed essentially the same way, and a full statement of changes in equity is required, reconciling each equity component from opening to closing balance. IFRS does not use the US par-value treasury-stock method, but the governing principle is identical: transactions with owners in their capacity as owners bypass profit or loss entirely.

Book value per share and stock subscriptions

Two smaller computations round out equity. Book value per common share = common stockholders’ equity (total equity minus the preferred claim, including any cumulative dividends in arrears) ÷ common shares outstanding — a balance-sheet measure distinct from market price or EPS. Stock subscriptions record a receivable when investors commit to buy shares before paying: debit Subscriptions receivable and credit Common stock subscribed plus APIC; the shares are issued only when fully paid, at which point the subscribed account is reclassified to common stock. The subscriptions receivable is presented as a contra-equity account rather than an asset, because it represents capital not yet contributed.

CMA bridge

CMA month 8 (corporate finance) used EPS in the financing decision and the EBIT/EPS indifference point; FAR is where the EPS number itself is computed, including the weighted-average share count and the basic-versus-diluted distinction.

Practice and recap

  1. Record stock issuance at par with the excess to APIC.
  2. Apply the cost method to treasury stock; no income-statement gain or loss.
  3. Capitalize small stock dividends at fair value, large at par; a split has no entry.
  4. Compute basic EPS as (NI − preferred dividends) ÷ weighted-average common shares; add only dilutive securities for diluted EPS.

Recap: equity transactions with owners never hit net income; small stock dividends use fair value and large ones use par; and basic EPS here is $3.00 — ($988,000 − $88,000) over 300,000 weighted-average shares — with diluted EPS always less than or equal to basic.

weeks.title: FAR U2·W4 — Bonds & Long-Term Liabilities (Effective Interest) (CPA Core · from CMA m8)
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — why a bond sells for less than its face

MBG's debt portfolio (the $310,000.00 from CMA month 8) and any bond financing share one mechanic: when a bond's stated rate differs from the market rate, it sells at a premium or discount, and the difference amortizes over the life using the effective-interest method. This is a guaranteed FAR computation.

Premium, discount, and carrying value

A bond pays interest at its stated (coupon) rate but investors price it at the market (effective) rate:

  • Stated rate < market rate → the bond sells at a discount (below face); investors demand more yield.
  • Stated rate > market rate → the bond sells at a premium (above face).
  • Stated rate = market rate → it sells at par.

The carrying value equals face value minus unamortized discount (or plus unamortized premium), and it moves toward face value over the bond's life.

The effective-interest method

Each period:

  • Interest expense = beginning carrying value × market (effective) rate.
  • Cash interest paid = face value × stated rate.
  • The difference amortizes the discount or premium.

Illustrative: a $1,000,000 face bond with a 5% stated rate (so $50,000 cash interest per year) is issued to yield 6% at a price of $960,000 (a $40,000 discount). Year 1 interest expense = $960,000 × 6% = $57,600; cash paid = $50,000; discount amortized = $57,600 − $50,000 = $7,600; new carrying value = $960,000 + $7,600 = $967,600. Because it is a discount, interest expense exceeds cash paid and the carrying value rises toward the $1,000,000 face. (A premium reverses this: expense is less than cash, and carrying value falls toward face.)

Other long-term liability points

Bond issue costs are recorded as a direct reduction of the carrying amount (like a discount) and amortized to interest expense. A bond retirement before maturity recognizes a gain or loss equal to the difference between the reacquisition price and the carrying value. Notes payable follow the same present-value logic. The straight-line method of amortization exists but the effective-interest method is GAAP-preferred because it produces a constant rate of interest on the carrying value.

Pricing a bond as a present value

A bond’s issue price is the present value of its cash flows discounted at the market rate: the present value of the face amount (a single sum) plus the present value of the coupon annuity. For the illustrative $1,000,000 bond paying 5% when the market yields 6%, the price is the PV of the $1,000,000 face at 6% plus the PV of the $50,000 coupons at 6% — which lands below face at the discount price the effective-interest schedule then amortizes. The point the exam rewards: the market rate, not the coupon, sets the price, while the coupon only fixes the cash interest. A semiannual bond halves both the rate and the coupon and doubles the number of periods.

Issuance between interest dates and bond issue costs

When a bond is sold between interest payment dates, the buyer pays the issuer the price plus accrued interest since the last coupon; that accrued amount is returned at the next full coupon, so it is not extra proceeds. Bond issue costs (underwriting, legal, printing) are presented as a direct deduction from the carrying amount — like a discount — and amortized to interest expense over the life, which nudges the effective rate slightly above the quoted market yield. This parallels how debt-issuance costs reduce the net liability rather than sitting as a separate asset.

Convertible bonds and detachable warrants

Two structures get special treatment. Convertible bonds under US GAAP are generally recorded entirely as debt — no proceeds are split out for the conversion feature — and on conversion the carrying value of the bonds becomes the basis of the stock issued (the book-value method), with no gain or loss. Bonds issued with detachable stock warrants, by contrast, do split the proceeds between the bond and the warrants (an equity instrument) by relative fair values, because the warrants trade separately. The distinction — convertibles stay all-debt, detachable warrants bifurcate — is a reliable exam point.

Classification, covenants, and extinguishment

Long-term debt is noncurrent only if the entity has both the intent and the ability to refinance or defer settlement beyond one year. If a borrower violates a covenant and the lender can call the debt, the obligation is reclassified to current under US GAAP unless the lender waives the right to demand repayment for more than a year from the balance-sheet date — and a waiver obtained after year-end but before the statements are issued (or available to be issued) can still support noncurrent classification. Under IFRS the waiver must be in place by the reporting (balance-sheet) date to keep the debt noncurrent; a post-reporting-date waiver does not help — a frequently tested GAAP/IFRS contrast. An early extinguishment recognizes a gain or loss equal to the reacquisition price versus the net carrying amount — including any unamortized discount, premium, and issue costs — in income from continuing operations. A troubled debt restructuring, where a lender grants a concession to a struggling borrower, is measured by comparing the carrying amount to the total future cash flows under the modified terms.

Imputed interest and the IFRS contrast

A noninterest-bearing or below-market note is not recorded at face — ASC 835 requires imputing interest at the market rate, recording the note at the present value of its payments and accreting the discount to interest expense over time, so the substance (a financing) overrides the stated low rate. IFRS contrast: IFRS measures financial liabilities at amortized cost using the same effective-interest method and folds transaction costs into the effective rate. The biggest divergence is convertibles: IAS 32 splits a convertible bond into a liability component and a separate equity component at issuance (the residual after valuing the liability at market), whereas US GAAP now typically leaves it all in debt. Both frameworks roll the carrying value toward face through the same effective-interest engine.

Straight-line versus effective interest, and serial bonds

Although the effective-interest method is GAAP-preferred, comparing it to straight-line sharpens the intuition. Straight-line amortizes the $40,000 discount evenly — for a five-year bond, $8,000 per year — producing constant interest expense of $50,000 + $8,000 = $58,000 each period. Effective interest instead produced $57,600 in year 1 and a rising expense thereafter as the carrying value climbs, holding the rate constant at 6% rather than the dollar amount. Over the full life both methods amortize the same total $40,000 and reach the same $1,000,000 maturity value; they differ only in timing. Serial bonds mature in installments rather than all at once, and a sinking fund sets aside restricted cash (a noncurrent investment) to retire principal — neither alters the effective-interest mechanic, but each changes how much principal remains outstanding to accrue interest on. Callable bonds let the issuer retire the debt early at a stated call price, with the difference between that call price and the carrying value recognized as the extinguishment gain or loss.

CMA bridge

CMA month 8 used the cost of debt and the after-tax rate in WACC; FAR is where the debt's carrying value and periodic interest expense are measured. The effective-interest mechanic here is the financial-accounting basis for the interest figure the finance computations rely on.

Practice and recap

  1. Determine premium/discount from stated vs market rate.
  2. Compute interest expense as carrying value × market rate.
  3. Amortize the difference between expense and cash paid; roll the carrying value toward face.
  4. Recognize a gain/loss on early retirement as reacquisition price vs carrying value.

Recap: a bond with a 5% coupon yielding 6% sells at a $40,000 discount; year-1 interest expense is $57,600, amortizing $7,600 of discount and lifting the carrying value to $967,600. Effective interest — carrying value times the market rate — is the GAAP-preferred method.

weeks.title: FAR U3·W1 — Statement of Cash Flows (CPA Core · from CMA m2/m8)
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — profit is not cash

MBG can post net income and still run short of cash — the CMA program's whole liquidity thread (months 2 and 8). The statement of cash flows reconciles the two by sorting every cash movement into three activities and reconciling net income to operating cash. FAR tests its structure, the classification of each item, and the indirect-method reconciliation.

Three sections

  • Operating — cash effects of transactions that enter net income (collections from customers, payments to suppliers and employees). Interest received, interest paid, and dividends received are operating under US GAAP.
  • Investing — buying and selling long-term assets and investments (equipment purchases, proceeds on disposals).
  • Financing — transactions with owners and lenders (issuing/repaying debt, issuing stock, paying dividends).

The classic trap: interest paid is operating, but dividends paid are financing.

Direct versus indirect

Only the operating section differs between methods. The direct method lists actual operating cash receipts and payments. The indirect method (far more common) starts with net income and adjusts for non-cash items and working-capital changes. Investing and financing sections are identical either way, and a reconciliation of net income to operating cash is required even under the direct method.

Indirect-method reconciliation

Starting from net income, add back non-cash expenses (depreciation, amortization), reverse gains/losses on asset sales (they belong in investing), and adjust for changes in operating working capital: an increase in a current asset uses cash (subtract), an increase in a current liability provides cash (add).

Illustrative: net income $988,000; + depreciation $80,000; − increase in accounts receivable $120,000; − increase in contract assets $100,000; + increase in accounts payable $60,000. Operating cash flow = $988,000 + $80,000 − $120,000 − $100,000 + $60,000 = $908,000. The $80,000 add-back is the same depreciation from FAR Unit 1; the contract-asset increase is the underbilling growth from ASC 606.

Non-cash and disclosures

Significant non-cash investing and financing activities — acquiring equipment with a capital lease, converting debt to equity, exchanging assets — are not in the body of the statement but are disclosed separately. Cash paid for interest and for income taxes is also disclosed under the indirect method. The statement reconciles beginning to ending cash and cash equivalents.

The direct method line by line

The direct method restates each accrual figure to its cash counterpart. Cash collected from customers = sales − the increase in accounts receivable (or plus a decrease). Cash paid to suppliers = cost of goods sold + the increase in inventory − the increase in accounts payable. Cash paid to employees = wage expense − the increase in wages payable. Cash paid for taxes = tax expense − the increase in income-taxes payable − the increase in a deferred tax liability + the increase in a deferred tax asset (signs reverse for decreases) — both deferred-tax movements back out the non-cash portion of tax expense. The sum of these cash flows equals the same operating total the indirect method reaches from net income — only the presentation differs. FASB encourages the direct method for clarity, but most filers choose indirect, which is why the indirect reconciliation is the one the exam drills hardest.

Finding investing cash flows from the accounts

Investing figures are usually reconstructed from asset accounts rather than handed to you. Suppose equipment that cost $90,000 with $50,000 of accumulated depreciation is sold at a $10,000 gain: proceeds = book value $40,000 + gain $10,000 = $50,000, reported as an investing inflow, while the $10,000 gain is subtracted in the operating section so it is not counted twice. Equipment purchases are found by rolling the gross asset account: beginning balance + purchases − cost of assets sold = ending balance. The same T-account logic recovers proceeds, purchases, and — with accumulated depreciation — the depreciation add-back, a favorite multi-step exam pattern.

Financing cash flows and non-cash conversions

The financing section captures changes in debt and equity for cash: issuing bonds or stock (inflows), repaying principal, repurchasing treasury shares, and paying dividends (outflows). Two subtleties recur. First, only the cash portion appears — converting bonds to stock or declaring a stock dividend are non-cash and are disclosed, not shown in the body. Second, dividends paid = dividends declared − the increase in dividends payable, because declaration and payment can straddle year-end. Repayment of principal is financing, but the interest on that same debt is operating — the split that catches the unwary.

Cash equivalents and special reconciling items

Cash equivalents are short-term, highly liquid investments with an original maturity of three months or less (Treasury bills, money-market funds); the statement reconciles beginning to ending cash and cash equivalents, so buying a T-bill is not an investing flow. Beyond depreciation, several non-cash items adjust the indirect reconciliation: equity-method income is subtracted (and dividends received added) because earnings exceed cash received; deferred tax expense is added back as a non-cash charge; stock-based compensation is added back; and amortization of a bond discount is added (it raised interest expense without cash). Each restates an accrual that moved net income but not cash.

IFRS contrast

IAS 7 permits more classification choice. Interest and dividends paid may be shown as either operating or financing, and interest and dividends received as either operating or investing, provided the choice is applied consistently — versus US GAAP, which fixes interest (paid and received) and dividends received in operating and dividends paid in financing. IFRS also allows bank overdrafts repayable on demand to be included within cash and cash equivalents, whereas US GAAP generally treats them as financing. Both frameworks allow the direct or indirect method and require the three-way operating/investing/financing structure, so the architecture is shared even where the line-item rules diverge.

A worked direct-method operating section

Tie the direct method back to the same facts. With operations producing $988,000 of net income, cash collected from customers is sales minus the $120,000 rise in receivables and the $100,000 growth in contract assets (an unbilled receivable, so it belongs in the collections bridge); cash paid for operating costs is the related expenses adjusted for the $60,000 rise in payables; and depreciation never appears because it is non-cash. When every operating receipt and payment is listed and netted, the direct method arrives at the identical $908,000 of operating cash the indirect reconciliation produced — proof that the two methods present one number, not two different results. Because a filer choosing the direct method must still show the indirect bridge, candidates have to be fluent in both directions: from net income to cash, and from each accrual line to its cash equivalent. A related analyst measure, free cash flow — operating cash flow minus capital expenditures — is not a required GAAP line but is built straight from this statement, underscoring why the cash-flow statement, not the income statement, is where liquidity is ultimately judged.

CMA bridge

CMA month 2 built the 13-week cash forecast and month 8 the cash conversion cycle; FAR formalizes the historical statement of cash flows with its three sections and the indirect reconciliation. The $80,000 depreciation and the contract-asset movement tie straight back to the FAR units before this.

Practice and recap

  1. Classify each cash flow as operating, investing, or financing (interest paid = operating; dividends paid = financing).
  2. Know that only the operating section differs between direct and indirect.
  3. Reconcile net income to operating cash: add non-cash items; increase in current asset subtract, increase in current liability add.
  4. Disclose significant non-cash investing/financing activities.

Recap: the statement sorts cash into operating, investing, and financing; the indirect method reconciles $988,000 of net income to $908,000 of operating cash by adding back $80,000 depreciation and adjusting working-capital changes — and interest paid is operating while dividends paid are financing.
