weeks.title: FAR U3·W2 — Governmental Accounting (CPA Core)
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — a different rulebook entirely

Governmental accounting is its own FAR world: a different standard-setter (GASB, not FASB), fund accounting, and a measurement basis that does not exist in business accounting. MBG itself is a private company, but state and local governments are major construction clients, so understanding how a municipality accounts for the project it hires MBG to build is genuinely useful — and it is heavily tested.

Fund accounting and the standard-setter

The Governmental Accounting Standards Board (GASB) sets standards for state and local governments. Governments account through funds — self-balancing sets of accounts for specific activities — grouped into three categories:

  • Governmental funds: general, special revenue, capital projects, debt service, and permanent funds.
  • Proprietary funds: enterprise (services to the public for a fee, e.g., a water utility) and internal service funds.
  • Fiduciary funds: custodial and trust funds held for others.

Two measurement focuses and bases

This is the heart of the topic:

  • Governmental funds use the current financial resources measurement focus and the modified accrual basis. They report fund balance, not net position, and record expenditures (not expenses).
  • Proprietary and fiduciary funds, and the government-wide statements, use the economic resources focus and full accrual basis — like a business.

Under modified accrual, revenue is recognized when it is measurable and available (collectible within the period or soon enough after — commonly within 60 days — to pay current liabilities), and expenditures are recognized when the related liability is incurred. So a long-lived asset purchase is an expenditure in full when acquired in a governmental fund, with no depreciation in that fund.

Government-wide versus fund statements

A government presents both government-wide statements (full accrual, economic resources, all activities together except fiduciary) and fund financial statements (governmental funds on modified accrual). A reconciliation bridges the two — for example, adding back capital assets and long-term debt that the fund statements do not carry. Encumbrance accounting reserves budgetary resources when a purchase order is issued, a budgetary control unique to governments.

The five governmental fund types

Within the governmental category each fund has a job. The General Fund accounts for all resources not required to be in another fund — the main operating fund. Special revenue funds account for revenues legally restricted to specific purposes (a gas-tax fund for road maintenance). Capital projects funds account for resources used to acquire or build major capital assets (the school a municipality hires a contractor to construct). Debt service funds accumulate resources to pay principal and interest on general long-term debt. Permanent funds report resources legally restricted so that only earnings, not principal, may be spent (a cemetery-care endowment). The capital assets built through a capital projects fund and the bonds that financed them do not sit in the fund — they appear only in the government-wide statements.

Fund balance classifications

GASB 54 sorts governmental-fund fund balance into a hierarchy reflecting how constrained the resources are: nonspendable (not in spendable form — inventory, prepaids, the principal of a permanent fund), restricted (constrained by external parties or law), committed (constrained by the government’s highest decision-making authority), assigned (intended for a purpose but not formally committed), and unassigned (the residual, found mainly in the General Fund). The classification communicates spending constraints to users and is a reliable exam item — distinguishing committed (formal action) from assigned (mere intent) in particular.

Nonexchange revenue recognition

Governments earn much revenue without an exchange, and GASB sorts these into four classes. Derived tax revenues (sales and income taxes) are recognized when the underlying transaction occurs. Imposed nonexchange revenues (property taxes, fines) are recognized in the period for which they are levied — property tax is recorded when an enforceable legal claim arises and recognized for the budget year it funds. Government-mandated and voluntary nonexchange transactions (grants) are recognized when all eligibility requirements are met. On modified accrual the additional available criterion still applies — revenue measurable but not yet available is deferred as a liability.

Budgetary accounting and encumbrances

Governments record their legally adopted budget in the accounts. The opening budgetary entry debits Estimated revenues, credits Appropriations (the spending authority), and books the difference to budgetary fund balance. During the year, issuing a purchase order records an encumbrance — debit Encumbrances, credit budgetary fund balance reserved for encumbrances — reserving appropriation so the government cannot overspend. When the goods arrive, the encumbrance is reversed and the actual expenditure and liability are recorded. Encumbrances are not expenditures and not GAAP-basis expenses; they are a budgetary control, and any outstanding at year-end are disclosed as commitments.

The government-wide statements and net position

The two government-wide statements use full accrual. The Statement of Net Position reports all assets and deferred outflows less liabilities and deferred inflows, with the residual net position split into net investment in capital assets, restricted, and unrestricted. The Statement of Activities uses a distinctive net-(expense)/revenue format: each function’s direct expenses are reduced by its program revenues (charges for services, operating and capital grants) to show the net cost borne by taxpayers, with general revenues (taxes) reported below. Fiduciary activities are excluded from the government-wide statements because the resources are not the government’s to use.

Reconciliation and the reporting package

Because the fund statements (modified accrual) and government-wide statements (full accrual) differ, a reconciliation bridges them: it adds back the capital assets (net of accumulated depreciation) and the long-term debt that governmental funds do not report, and converts capital-outlay and debt-principal expenditures back to the accrual measures. The full annual report — the Annual Comprehensive Financial Report (ACFR) — wraps the basic statements with Management’s Discussion and Analysis (MD&A) and other required supplementary information (RSI) such as the budgetary comparison schedule. Proprietary funds add a statement of cash flows with four categories (operating, noncapital financing, capital and related financing, and investing) — note the two financing categories, unlike the single financing section in business accounting.

Interfund activity and capital project flows

Resources move between funds, and the labels matter. Interfund transfers (the General Fund subsidizing a debt service fund) are reported as other financing sources/uses, not revenues or expenditures. Interfund loans create a due-to/due-from and are not revenue at all. When a city issues bonds in a capital projects fund to build a school, the proceeds are an other financing source — the fund records no long-term liability, since that debt appears only government-wide — and the construction payments to the contractor are expenditures as incurred. The matching debt service fund later records principal and interest as expenditures only when due and payable, not as they accrue — another modified-accrual hallmark. Special items and significant one-time flows, when present, are reported separately below the normal revenues and expenditures so users can see them distinctly.

CMA bridge

CMA taught accrual job-cost accounting for a private builder; governmental accounting flips several assumptions — modified accrual, expenditures instead of expenses, and no depreciation in governmental funds. Recognizing where business GAAP does and does not apply is the exam skill.

Practice and recap

  1. Know GASB sets state/local government standards and the three fund categories.
  2. Governmental funds: current financial resources + modified accrual + expenditures.
  3. Proprietary/fiduciary and government-wide: economic resources + full accrual.
  4. Modified-accrual revenue = measurable and available; reconcile fund to government-wide statements.

Recap: governments use fund accounting under GASB; governmental funds run on modified accrual (revenue when measurable and available, expenditures when incurred, no depreciation) while proprietary funds and the government-wide statements use full accrual.

weeks.title: FAR U3·W3 — Not-for-Profit Accounting (CPA Core)
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — two net-asset buckets, not retained earnings

Not-for-profit entities (charities, foundations, private universities, many hospitals) follow FASB but with their own twists: equity is called net assets and split by donor restriction, and contributions are the defining transaction. The construction connection is real — MBG-style builders frequently work for nonprofits and faith-based developers — and FAR tests NFP every form.

Two classes of net assets

Under current standards, an NFP reports just two classes of net assets:

  • Net assets without donor restrictions — available for any purpose at the board's discretion.
  • Net assets with donor restrictions — limited by donors as to purpose or time (including permanently restricted endowments).

When a donor restriction is satisfied (the purpose is fulfilled or the time passes), the amount is reclassified from net assets with donor restrictions to net assets without donor restrictions — shown as a "net assets released from restrictions" line.

Contributions

A contribution is an unconditional, nonreciprocal transfer of assets. It is recognized as revenue at fair value when received or unconditionally promised (a pledge). Classify it by whether the donor imposed a restriction.

A conditional contribution — one with a barrier the NFP must overcome and a right of return if it does not — is not recognized until the condition is substantially met; cash received in advance is a refundable liability. Distinguish a condition (a barrier) from a restriction (a donor limit on use): a conditional gift is not yet revenue, while a restricted gift is revenue now, just in the restricted class.

Exchange versus contribution

An exchange transaction is reciprocal — the NFP provides commensurate value (tuition, a service fee) — and follows ASC 606 revenue recognition. A contribution is nonreciprocal. Many transactions are part-exchange, part-contribution (a $500 gala ticket for a $100 dinner has a $400 contribution element).

Statements and donated items

NFPs present a statement of financial position, a statement of activities, and a statement of cash flows; expenses are reported by function (program services vs supporting — management and general, and fundraising) and by nature. Donated services are recognized only if they create or enhance a nonfinancial asset, or require specialized skills the donor possesses and the NFP would otherwise buy. Donated materials are recognized at fair value.

Endowments and UPMIFA

An endowment is a fund meant to be invested with the principal preserved. A donor-restricted endowment (the donor requires principal be held permanently or for a term) sits in net assets with donor restrictions; a board-designated endowment — a quasi-endowment — is the board’s own earmarking of unrestricted funds and stays in net assets without donor restrictions, because a board can reverse its own designation. Most states’ UPMIFA statute governs spending: absent explicit donor terms, the original gift amount is classified as restricted and appreciation is restricted until appropriated for spending. An underwater endowment — fair value below the original gift — is still reported within net assets with donor restrictions, with the shortfall disclosed.

Promises to give and investment return

Unconditional promises to give collectible in future years are recorded at the present value of expected cash flows, with the discount accreted to contribution revenue over time, and reduced by an allowance for uncollectible pledges. Investment returns — interest, dividends, and realized and unrealized gains on endowment and other investments — are reported net of external and direct internal investment expenses and classified by the presence or absence of donor restrictions on the income. A donor may restrict the income of an endowment even when the principal is permanent, so the return can land in either net-asset class depending on the gift terms.

Required statements and functional expenses

Every NFP must present an analysis of expenses by both function and natural classification — historically a separate statement of functional expenses, now required of all NFPs in some form (statement, schedule, or notes). Functions divide into program services (the mission) and supporting services (management and general, fundraising, and membership development). Costs that benefit more than one function are allocated, and the methods are disclosed; the program-to-supporting ratio is a metric donors and watchdogs scrutinize. The core statements remain the statement of financial position, the statement of activities (showing the change in each net-asset class), and the statement of cash flows.

Liquidity, agency transactions, and contributed assets

ASU 2016-14 added a required liquidity and availability disclosure: qualitative information on how the NFP manages liquidity plus a quantitative measure of financial assets available within one year to meet general expenditures, since donor restrictions can lock up resources. An agency (pass-through) transaction — where the NFP receives assets to transfer to a specified third party — is not contribution revenue; the NFP records a liability to the ultimate beneficiary. A gift of a long-lived asset (or cash restricted to acquire one) may be released from restriction either when placed in service or over the asset’s useful life, depending on the NFP’s accounting policy.

Healthcare NFPs and the bottom line

Not-for-profit healthcare entities add wrinkles: they report a performance indicator (analogous to income from operations) on the statement of operations, present patient service revenue net of contractual adjustments with explicit and implicit price concessions, and recognize charity care as a disclosure only (no revenue) because payment was never expected. Across all NFPs the through-line is the same: equity is net assets viewed through the lens of donor intent, contributions — not retained earnings — drive the change in net assets, and the statements exist to show whether the organization honored the restrictions attached to the resources entrusted to it.

Split-interest gifts and special events

Two recurring NFP transactions round out the picture. A split-interest agreement — a charitable remainder trust or charitable gift annuity — gives the NFP a future interest while another beneficiary receives payments for a time; the NFP recognizes contribution revenue for the present value of its expected residual interest and a liability for amounts owed to the other beneficiary, remeasured as actuarial assumptions update. A special event such as a gala is split into its exchange and contribution elements: the fair value of the direct benefit to the attendee (the meal) is exchange revenue, and the excess paid is a contribution. Worked split: a $500 gala ticket where the dinner’s fair value is $90 yields $90 of exchange revenue and a $410 contribution — and it is the fair value received, not whether the attendee shows up, that fixes the split. The direct costs of the benefit may be netted against special-event revenue or shown as a cost of supporting services, with the policy disclosed. These mechanics reinforce the unit’s core test — separate what the donor gave freely from what they received in return, and recognize each under its own rule.

CMA bridge

The contribution-recognition logic mirrors ASC 606's control and condition concepts from FAR Unit 1, and the functional-expense split parallels the responsibility-center thinking from CMA month 3 — here the categories are program versus supporting services.

Practice and recap

  1. Report two net-asset classes: with and without donor restrictions.
  2. Recognize contributions at fair value when unconditional; reclassify when restrictions are met.
  3. Do not recognize conditional contributions until the barrier is overcome.
  4. Separate exchange transactions (ASC 606) from contributions; report expenses by function.

Recap: NFPs split net assets into with- and without-donor-restriction classes, recognize unconditional contributions at fair value now and reclassify on release, defer conditional gifts until the barrier is met, and report expenses by function.

weeks.title: FAR U3·W4 — Accounting Changes, Errors, Interim & Segment Reporting (CPA Core)
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — restate, adjust, or just go forward?

When MBG changes how it accounts for something — or discovers a prior mistake — FAR prescribes exactly one of three treatments, and choosing the wrong one is a classic exam miss. The rule turns on whether it is a change in principle, a change in estimate, or an error. This week settles all three and adds interim and segment reporting.

The three treatments (ASC 250)

  • Change in accounting principle — switching from one acceptable GAAP method to another (e.g., FIFO to weighted-average inventory). Apply it retrospectively: restate prior periods presented and adjust the opening balance of retained earnings for the earliest period.
  • Change in accounting estimate — revising a judgment as new information arrives (useful life, salvage, bad-debt rate, warranty rate). Apply it prospectively: current and future periods only; do not touch prior periods.
  • Error correction — a mistake in previously issued statements (math error, misapplied GAAP, overlooked facts). Restate the prior periods (a prior-period adjustment to beginning retained earnings).

The depreciation-method trap

A change in depreciation method (say, double-declining-balance to straight-line) looks like a change in principle but is treated as a change in estimate effected by a change in principle — so it is accounted for prospectively, not retrospectively. This is one of FAR's favorite distractors: it is the prior estimate of how the asset is consumed that is changing.

A change in reporting entity (e.g., changing the entities in consolidated statements) is applied retrospectively, like a principle change.

Counterbalancing errors

Some errors counterbalance — they self-correct over two periods (e.g., an inventory misstatement reverses the next year). If found after two years and the books are closed, no entry is needed for the income effect, though prior-period statements presented still need correcting. Non-counterbalancing errors (e.g., a depreciation error) persist until fixed.

Interim and segment reporting

Interim reporting (ASC 270) generally treats each interim period as an integral part of the annual period: income taxes, for instance, use the estimated annual effective tax rate applied to year-to-date income. Segment reporting (ASC 280) uses the management approach — segments are reported the way management runs the business — and a segment is reportable if it meets any 10% threshold of total revenue, profit or loss, or assets, with reported segments covering at least 75% of external revenue.

Retrospective application and its limits

Applying a principle change retrospectively means restating each prior period presented as if the new method had always been used, and adjusting the opening retained earnings of the earliest period shown for the cumulative effect on still-earlier years. Only the direct effects (and related income-tax effects) are restated; indirect effects — such as a profit-sharing accrual that would have differed — are recognized in the period of change, not restated. When it is impracticable to determine the period-specific or cumulative effect (the data simply do not exist), the change is applied prospectively from the earliest practicable date — an explicit exception the exam tests against students who assume retrospective is always possible.

Disclosures and the justification requirement

A voluntary change in principle is permitted only if the new method is preferable, and management must justify that preferability — you cannot switch methods to smooth earnings at will. The change is disclosed with its nature and reason, the method of applying it, and the effect on income, per-share amounts, and affected line items for each period presented. A material change in estimate is disclosed as to its effect, and an error correction is disclosed as a restatement, including the nature of the error and the effect on each prior period and on opening retained earnings. This audit-trail discipline mirrors the integrity controls emphasized throughout the program.

Interim reporting — integral view and exceptions

Treating an interim period as an integral part of the year drives several rules. The estimated annual effective tax rate is re-estimated each quarter and applied year-to-date, so a later quarter catches up any change. Some costs that benefit the whole year may be allocated across interim periods. But several items are recognized discretely, in the period they occur: a permanent inventory write-down (a temporary market decline expected to reverse by year-end is not recognized), a loss contingency, and a LIFO liquidation expected to be replaced by year-end (interim cost of sales includes the expected replacement cost). Publicly traded companies present condensed interim statements under SEC rules, with minimum disclosures emphasizing seasonality and significant changes.

Segment reporting mechanics

Under the management approach, operating segments are the components whose results the chief operating decision maker reviews to allocate resources. A segment is reportable if it meets any one of three 10% tests: its revenue (including intersegment) is 10% or more of combined revenue; the absolute value of its profit or loss is 10% or more of the greater (in absolute value) of total segment profit or total segment loss; or its assets are 10% or more of combined segment assets. If the reportable segments’ combined external revenue is below 75% of consolidated revenue, add segments until the 75% threshold is met. Segments similar in economics and other factors may be aggregated.

A worked threshold and entity-wide disclosures

Worked test: total combined segment revenue is $10,000,000. A division with $1,300,000 of revenue clears the 10% revenue test ($1,300,000 > $1,000,000) and is reportable even if it runs at a loss, because any single 10% test suffices. Beyond segment detail, ASC 280 requires entity-wide disclosures regardless of segments: revenues from external customers by product or service and by geographic area (domestic versus foreign, with material individual countries), long-lived assets by geography, and the existence of any major customer providing 10% or more of total revenue (with the amount and segment, though the customer need not be named). These reveal the concentration information consolidated totals hide.

A worked counterbalancing error

Suppose ending inventory in Year 1 is understated by $30,000. Understated ending inventory overstates cost of goods sold and understates Year 1 net income by $30,000. Because Year 1 ending inventory is Year 2 beginning inventory, Year 2 cost of goods sold is understated and Year 2 net income is overstated by the same $30,000 — the error counterbalances, leaving retained earnings correct by the end of Year 2. If discovered during Year 2 before closing, correct both years; if discovered after Year 2 closes, retained earnings has already self-corrected and no income adjustment is needed, though any comparative statements still shown must be restated. A non-counterbalancing error — for example, capitalizing an item that should have been expensed — does not self-correct and must be fixed whenever found.

CMA bridge

CMA month 3 covered segment reporting for performance; FAR adds the ASC 280 quantitative thresholds and the management approach. The estimate-versus-principle distinction echoes the relevant-cost discipline — know precisely which rule applies before you compute.

Practice and recap

  1. Change in principle → retrospective; change in estimate → prospective; error → restate.
  2. A depreciation-method change is a change in estimate (prospective).
  3. Recognize counterbalancing errors that self-correct over two periods.
  4. Interim tax uses the estimated annual effective rate; segments use the management approach and 10% thresholds.

Recap: retrospective for principle and reporting-entity changes, prospective for estimates (including depreciation-method changes), and restatement for errors — while interim periods apply the estimated annual effective tax rate and segments follow the management approach with 10% reportability thresholds.

units.title: AUD Unit 1 — Engagements & Ethics, the Audit Risk Model & Internal Control

weeks.title: AUD U1·W1 — Engagements, Ethics & Independence (CPA Core · from CMA m5/m12)
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — who can audit MBG, and how independent must they be?

Auditing begins before any testing: the right engagement type, the auditor's ethics, and — above all — independence. CMA month 12 covered the IMA ethics standards from the preparer's side; AUD covers the AICPA Code from the auditor's side. The recurring exam theme is that an auditor's value comes entirely from being, and appearing, independent.

Levels of assurance and engagement types

  • Audit — the highest level, reasonable assurance, expressed as a positive opinion that the statements are fairly presented in accordance with the framework.
  • Review — limited (negative) assurance: "we are not aware of any material modifications needed." Based mainly on inquiry and analytical procedures.
  • Compilation — no assurance; the accountant assembles statements from management's data.
  • Examination / agreed-upon procedures — attestation engagements at varying assurance.

Reasonable assurance is high but not absolute — an audit is designed to detect material misstatement, not every error, because of sampling, judgment, and the nature of evidence.

The AICPA Code of Professional Conduct

Core principles: integrity, objectivity, independence, due care, and professional skepticism. The conceptual framework approach asks the CPA to identify threats to compliance (self-interest, self-review, advocacy, familiarity, undue influence) and apply safeguards that reduce them to an acceptable level. Professional skepticism — a questioning mind and critical assessment of evidence — runs through the entire audit.

Independence in fact and in appearance

Independence has two dimensions: in fact (an actual unbiased mindset) and in appearance (a reasonable, informed third party would conclude the auditor is unbiased). Both are required. A covered member generally may not have a direct financial interest, or a material indirect interest, in an attest client; may not have certain loans or business relationships; and may not perform management functions for the client. Performing the client's bookkeeping and then auditing it is a self-review threat that typically impairs independence for an issuer.

For MBG's auditor, independence would be impaired by owning an interest in MBG, by a partner's spouse working in MBG's finance function, or by the firm having set up MBG's books and now opining on them. Note independence is required for attest engagements (audit, review, examination) but not for a pure compilation or for non-attest tax/consulting work — though objectivity and integrity always apply.

Engagement acceptance and the preconditions for an audit

Before accepting, the auditor confirms the preconditions: management uses an acceptable financial-reporting framework and acknowledges its responsibility for the statements, for internal control, and for giving the auditor access to evidence. The terms are set in an engagement letter — the contract documenting the objective and scope, each party’s responsibilities, the inherent limitations, and the framework. For a first-year engagement the successor auditor must, with client permission, communicate with the predecessor auditor about disagreements, fraud or illegal acts, and the reason for the change; the client’s refusal to permit that contact is itself a red flag weighing against acceptance.

Independence frameworks beyond the AICPA

Three rule sets can apply at once. The AICPA Code governs private-company attest work through the threats-and-safeguards framework. For issuers, the stricter SEC and PCAOB rules add: a prohibition on most non-audit services (bookkeeping, financial-system design, internal-audit outsourcing, valuation, and management functions for the same audit client), mandatory audit-partner rotation (lead and concurring partners rotate off after five years), audit-committee pre-approval of all services, and a one-year cooling-off period before an audit-team member can take a key financial-reporting role at the client. Government audits add the GAO’s Yellow Book, whose conceptual framework parallels the AICPA but treats preparing the financial statements as a significant self-review threat requiring safeguards.

Financial interests, family, and employment

The detail of who and what impairs independence is heavily tested. A direct financial interest in an attest client impairs independence regardless of amount; an indirect interest (through a mutual fund, say) impairs only if material. Immediate family (spouse, dependents) are generally subject to the same restrictions as the covered member, so a spouse’s direct investment in the client impairs independence, and a spouse’s employment with the client impairs it if the spouse holds a key position. Close relatives (parents, siblings, nondependent children) impair independence in narrower circumstances — a key-position role or a material financial interest the covered member knows of. Most loans to or from a client impair independence, with narrow exceptions (a car loan or a fully collateralized mortgage from a financial-institution client on normal terms).

Fees, confidentiality, and acts discreditable

Several rules protect objectivity beyond independence. Contingent fees and commissions are prohibited for attest clients, because tying the fee to a result corrupts judgment; they are permitted for some non-attest clients with disclosure. The confidential client information rule bars disclosing client data without consent, subject to exceptions (a valid subpoena, a peer review, an authorized regulatory body). Acts discreditable — retaining client records to coerce payment, discrimination, or signing a materially false return — violate the Code regardless of independence. A CPA must also exercise due professional care, working with the competence and diligence of a reasonably prudent practitioner.

Quality management at the firm level

Independence is reinforced by firm-wide quality management. Under the AICPA’s quality-management standards (and PCAOB standards for issuers), a firm designs a system addressing leadership and the tone at the top, relevant ethical requirements including independence, acceptance and continuance of clients, engagement performance, resources, and monitoring and remediation. An engagement quality review — an objective partner not on the engagement reviewing significant judgments and the report before issuance — is required for issuer audits and certain others. The thread tying the week together: the auditor’s opinion is worth nothing unless the firm and the individual are competent, objective, and independent in both fact and appearance — everything in the rest of the audit assumes it.

The period of independence and network firms

Independence must be maintained throughout both the period of the professional engagement and the period covered by the financial statements, so a financial interest held even before the engagement letter is signed can impair independence for the year under audit. The rules also reach beyond the individual firm: in an alliance or network of firms, other network firms must be independent of an audit client where it is reasonable to expect the network is associated with the engagement. When an independence problem is discovered, the firm evaluates its significance, applies safeguards or removes the affected individuals, and documents the resolution. Independence is ultimately judged from the perspective of a reasonable and informed third party weighing all the facts — not from the auditor’s own belief that they remain objective.

CMA bridge

CMA month 12's IMA standards (integrity, credibility) parallel the AICPA principles; the difference is the auditor's independence requirement, which has no exact CMA counterpart because the management accountant is internal. Both, though, demand objectivity and a refusal to misrepresent.

Practice and recap

  1. Match engagement type to assurance level: audit (reasonable/positive), review (limited/negative), compilation (none).
  2. Apply the AICPA principles and the threats-and-safeguards framework; maintain professional skepticism.
  3. Require independence in fact and in appearance for attest engagements.
  4. Identify relationships that impair independence (financial interest, self-review, management functions).

Recap: an audit gives reasonable (not absolute) assurance via a positive opinion; the AICPA Code centers on integrity, objectivity, due care, skepticism, and — uniquely — independence in fact and appearance, which bookkeeping-then-auditing or a financial interest in the client would impair.

weeks.title: AUD U1·W2 — The Audit Risk Model & Materiality (CPA Core · from CMA m10)
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — how much testing is enough?

The audit risk model is the engine that answers "how much evidence do we need?" It links the risk of material misstatement to the amount of substantive testing the auditor must perform. CMA month 10 assessed business risk; AUD turns risk assessment into a testing plan through this model and the materiality thresholds that frame it.

The audit risk model

Audit risk = Inherent risk × Control risk × Detection risk.

  • Audit risk (AR) — the risk the auditor gives an unmodified opinion on materially misstated statements. The auditor sets it low (commonly ~5%).
  • Inherent risk (IR) — susceptibility to misstatement before controls (estimates, complex transactions). The auditor assesses but cannot change it.
  • Control risk (CR) — risk that internal control fails to prevent/detect a misstatement. Assessed, not controlled by the auditor.
  • Detection risk (DR) — risk the auditor's procedures fail to catch a misstatement. This is the only component the auditor controls, by changing the nature, timing, and extent of substantive procedures.

Solving for detection risk

Rearranging: DR = AR ÷ (IR × CR). The product IR × CR is the risk of material misstatement (RMM). Illustrative: target AR 5%, IR 80%, CR 50%. RMM = 0.80 × 0.50 = 40%. DR = 0.05 ÷ 0.40 = 0.125 (12.5%).

The key relationship is inverse: the higher the RMM, the lower the acceptable detection risk, which means the auditor must do more and better substantive testing — larger samples, more reliable evidence, and procedures performed at year-end rather than interim. When controls are strong (low CR), the auditor can accept higher DR and test less substantively (after testing those controls).

Materiality

Misstatements matter only if they could influence users' decisions. The auditor sets:

  • Overall (planning) materiality — usually a percentage of a benchmark (pre-tax income, revenue, or total assets) appropriate to the entity.
  • Performance materiality — set below overall materiality to reduce the chance that the aggregate of undetected and uncorrected misstatements exceeds overall materiality.
  • Clearly trivial threshold — amounts below which misstatements need not be accumulated.

Materiality has a quantitative and a qualitative side: a small misstatement can be material if it changes a loss to a profit, hides a trend, or affects debt covenants — exactly the kind of bank-covenant sensitivity MBG's surety and lenders watch.

Risk assessment procedures

The auditor does not guess at inherent and control risk — they are grounded in required risk assessment procedures: obtaining an understanding of the entity and its environment (industry, regulation, business model), its internal control, and the applicable framework. The procedures are inquiry of management and others, analytical procedures, observation, and inspection of documents. Risk assessment procedures alone do not provide sufficient audit evidence for an opinion — they direct where the substantive work goes. A required part of this phase is the engagement team discussion (the brainstorming session) about where the statements are susceptible to material misstatement, including from fraud.

Assertions — the unit of audit risk

Risk and materiality ultimately attach to management assertions embedded in the statements, and procedures are designed assertion by assertion. For account balances: existence, completeness, rights and obligations, and valuation/allocation. For transactions: occurrence, completeness, accuracy, cutoff, and classification. For presentation and disclosure: occurrence and rights, completeness, accuracy/valuation, and understandability. The auditor maps each significant risk to the specific assertion at stake — for a contractor, the existence of recorded receivables and the cutoff and accuracy of percentage-of-completion revenue are typically the assertions most at risk.

Significant risks and the revenue presumption

Some risks demand special audit consideration. A significant risk — one with higher inherent risk due to complexity, subjectivity, or fraud potential — requires substantive procedures specifically responsive to it and prohibits relying on prior-period control testing without re-testing the controls. Auditing standards presume revenue recognition is a fraud risk unless that presumption is rebutted, because revenue is the account most often manipulated; for a contractor that means heightened scrutiny of estimated costs to complete and the timing of recognized revenue. Significant risks frequently involve accounting estimates with measurement uncertainty, where the auditor evaluates the data, assumptions, and method management used.

From risk to response — nature, timing, extent

The assessed risk drives the further audit procedures along three dimensions. Nature: more reliable evidence for higher risk — external confirmations and inspection over inquiry, and tests of detail over analytics. Timing: testing at year-end rather than interim when risk is high, since interim testing leaves a roll-forward gap. Extent: larger sample sizes as the desired detection risk falls. Procedures are either tests of controls (do the controls operate?) or substantive procedures (tests of detail and substantive analytics); a dual-purpose test does both at once. The auditor responds to financial-statement-level risk with overall responses (more experienced staff, heightened skepticism) and to assertion-level risk with specific procedures.

Analytical procedures and revisiting materiality

Analytical procedures — evaluating financial data through plausible relationships — are required in the risk-assessment (planning) phase and again in the final review near the end of the audit to form an overall conclusion; they are optional as a substantive procedure during fieldwork. Materiality is not static: if the auditor learns the benchmark was wrong (actual income differs sharply from the estimate used), materiality is revised and the planned procedures reconsidered. At the end, the auditor accumulates identified misstatements, compares them to materiality, and asks management to correct them — uncorrected misstatements above the clearly-trivial threshold are evaluated, individually and in aggregate, against overall materiality to decide whether the opinion must be modified. Risk and materiality thus bracket the entire audit: they size the work at the start and judge the result at the finish.

Sufficient appropriate evidence and sampling

The output of the risk model is a plan to gather sufficient appropriate audit evidence — sufficiency is the quantity (more is needed as risk rises) and appropriateness is the quality, comprising relevance (does it address the assertion?) and reliability (higher when from independent external sources, under effective controls, in documentary form, or obtained directly by the auditor). Evidence from a knowledgeable source outside the entity, such as a bank confirmation, outweighs the same fact asserted only by management. Because testing every item is rarely economical, the auditor often uses audit sampling, accepting a measured sampling risk that the sample is not representative; lowering the tolerable detection risk drives larger samples. The model, the assertions, materiality, and the evidence standard thus form one chain: risk sets how much and how good the evidence must be, and sampling delivers it efficiently.

CMA bridge

CMA month 10 quantified business risk (likelihood × impact, VaR); AUD's risk model is the audit analogue — assess inherent and control risk, then set detection risk to hold audit risk low. The mindset is identical: more risk demands more rigor.

Practice and recap

  1. Know AR = IR × CR × DR and that DR is the only component the auditor controls.
  2. Compute DR = AR ÷ (IR × CR); RMM = IR × CR.
  3. Apply the inverse relationship: higher RMM → lower DR → more substantive testing.
  4. Set overall and (lower) performance materiality; weigh qualitative materiality.

Recap: with AR 5%, IR 80%, and CR 50%, the risk of material misstatement is 40% and detection risk must be 12.5% — a low DR that forces extensive substantive testing. Performance materiality sits below overall materiality, and small misstatements can still be qualitatively material.

weeks.title: AUD U1·W3 — Internal Control & Fraud in the Audit (CPA Core · from CMA m5/m12)
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — MBG's transaction registry, seen by the auditor

CMA months 5 and 12 built MBG's controls — segregation of duties and the VERIFIED/POSTED/FLAGGED transaction registry. AUD looks at those same controls from outside: the auditor must understand internal control, decide whether to rely on it, and stay alert to fraud, including management's ability to override the very controls that look strong on paper.

Understanding and testing internal control

On every audit, the auditor must obtain an understanding of internal control relevant to the audit — all five COSO components: control environment, risk assessment, control activities, information and communication, and monitoring. Understanding is required even if the auditor does not plan to rely on controls.

To rely on controls (assess control risk below maximum and reduce substantive testing), the auditor must test their operating effectiveness with tests of controls. Tests of controls ask "did the control operate?"; substantive procedures ask "is the balance correct?" If controls are ineffective or the auditor chooses not to rely on them, control risk is high and substantive testing increases (the model from last week).

The integrated audit (SOX)

For issuers, Sarbanes-Oxley §404 and PCAOB standards can require an integrated audit in which the auditor opines on both the financial statements and the effectiveness of internal control over financial reporting (ICFR). The auditor’s ICFR attestation under §404(b) applies only to issuers that are accelerated or large accelerated filers; nonaccelerated filers and eligible smaller reporting companies are exempt from the auditor attestation, though management still performs its own §404(a) assessment. A material weakness (a reasonable possibility of a material misstatement not being prevented or detected) yields an adverse ICFR opinion. A private company like MBG is not subject to §404, but the same control concepts drive the financial-statement audit.

Fraud and professional skepticism (AU-C 240)

Two fraud types: fraudulent financial reporting (intentional misstatement to deceive users) and misappropriation of assets (theft). The fraud triangle from CMA month 12 — pressure, opportunity, rationalization — drives the auditor's risk assessment. Required procedures include an engagement-team brainstorming about how fraud could occur, inquiries of management and others, and a rebuttable presumption that improper revenue recognition is a fraud risk (the auditor may overcome it only with documented reasons).

Critically, the auditor must always address the risk of management override of controls — even strong controls can be overridden by those who design them. Required responses include testing journal entries (especially nonstandard, period-end, and round-dollar entries), reviewing accounting estimates for bias, and evaluating significant unusual transactions. Professional skepticism means not accepting evidence at face value just because management seems honest.

The five components and control activities

Each COSO component does specific work. The control environment is the tone at the top — integrity, board oversight, competence. Risk assessment is management’s own identification of risks to reporting. Control activities are the policies that address those risks: authorization, segregation of duties (separating authorization, recording, and custody), physical controls over assets and records, reconciliations, and performance reviews. Information and communication captures and shares the data that make controls run, and monitoring evaluates whether controls keep working over time. MBG’s segregation of duties is a control activity; its transaction registry is part of information and communication and supports monitoring.

Design, implementation, and walkthroughs

Understanding control is not one question but three. The auditor evaluates whether a control is designed effectively (would it prevent or detect a misstatement?) and whether it has been implemented (does it actually exist and operate?) — assessed through inquiry combined with observation, inspection, or a walkthrough that traces one transaction from origination through the records. Only when the auditor intends to rely on a control does it additionally test operating effectiveness over the period. Design-and-implementation work is required on every audit; operating-effectiveness testing is required only for reliance (and, for issuers, for the ICFR opinion).

Deficiencies and required communications

Control problems are graded by severity. A control deficiency exists when a control does not let management or employees prevent or detect misstatements on a timely basis. A significant deficiency is important enough to merit the attention of those charged with governance. A material weakness is the most severe — a reasonable possibility that a material misstatement would not be prevented or detected — and, for an issuer, forces an adverse ICFR opinion. The auditor must communicate significant deficiencies and material weaknesses in writing to those charged with governance, and that communication is required even if the deficiencies were remediated during the year.

The inherent limitations of any control system

No system of internal control gives absolute assurance, and the exam tests why. Management override lets those who design the controls bypass them; collusion between two or more people defeats segregation of duties; human error and faulty judgment cause breakdowns; and cost-benefit constraints mean management will not control immaterial risks. These limitations are precisely why an auditor cannot rely on controls alone and must always perform some substantive procedures, and why even a clean ICFR opinion is reasonable, not absolute, assurance. They also explain the standing requirement to address management override regardless of how strong the controls appear.

IT controls, service organizations, and illegal acts

Most controls today are embedded in systems. IT general controls (ITGCs) — over access and security, program change management, and computer operations — underpin the application controls (edit checks, validations, automated reconciliations) the auditor may rely on; weak ITGCs can undermine otherwise sound application controls. When a client outsources a process (payroll, hosting) to a service organization, the auditor obtains a SOC 1 report from the service auditor: a type 1 covers design at a point in time, a type 2 covers operating effectiveness over a period, and only a type 2 supports reliance on those controls. Finally, the auditor considers laws and regulations: noncompliance with a direct effect on the statements is audited like any other misstatement, and the auditor responds to identified or suspected noncompliance by evaluating the effect and communicating to the appropriate level — escalating to those charged with governance when senior management is involved.

Communicating and documenting fraud findings

When the auditor identifies fraud or a suspicion of it, the communication path depends on who is involved and how material it is. Any fraud involving senior management, or fraud that causes a material misstatement, is communicated to those charged with governance; even immaterial fraud by an employee is reported to the appropriate level of management. The auditor’s normal duty of confidentiality may yield to a duty to disclose outside the entity in limited circumstances (a successor auditor with client consent, a subpoena, a regulator). Throughout, the auditor maintains professional skepticism and documents the fraud risk assessment, the brainstorming, the responses, and the basis for conclusions — the work that lets a later reviewer confirm the override and revenue-recognition risks were genuinely addressed rather than assumed away. If the risk is so severe that the auditor can no longer rely on management’s representations, withdrawal from the engagement may be the only appropriate response.

CMA bridge

CMA framed segregation of duties and the transaction registry as fraud prevention (denying opportunity); AUD adds the auditor's detection responsibility — test the controls, and never assume they cannot be overridden from the top.

Practice and recap

  1. Obtain an understanding of all five COSO components on every audit.
  2. To rely on controls, test their operating effectiveness; otherwise increase substantive testing.
  3. For issuers, perform an integrated audit of ICFR; a material weakness → adverse ICFR opinion.
  4. Assess fraud risk (triangle), presume revenue-recognition fraud, and always address management override by testing journal entries.

Recap: the auditor understands internal control on every engagement and tests it only to rely on it; issuers get an integrated ICFR audit; and fraud work — brainstorming, the revenue-recognition presumption, and journal-entry testing for management override — runs on professional skepticism.

weeks.title: REG U1·W1 — Ethics, Professional Responsibilities & Federal Tax Procedures (CPA Core · from CMA m12)
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — the tax preparer's own rulebook

REG is the CPA section where you become the tax adviser, and before any number reaches a return there is a body of rules governing how a preparer must behave. When Jordan Reed's construction company MBG files its returns, the CPA who signs them is bound by Treasury Circular 230, the Internal Revenue Code's preparer-penalty regime, and the AICPA Statements on Standards for Tax Services. CMA month 12 covered ethics from the management accountant's seat; REG adds the tax practitioner's distinct duties and the real penalties for breaching them.

Circular 230 — practice before the IRS

Circular 230 is issued by the Treasury Department and governs who may practice before the IRS and how. Those with unlimited practice rights are attorneys, CPAs, and enrolled agents (EAs); enrolled actuaries and enrolled retirement plan agents have limited rights. A practitioner's core duties include exercising due diligence as to the accuracy of returns and representations; promptly submitting records the IRS lawfully requests; not charging an unconscionable fee and not charging a contingent fee except in narrow situations (such as an examination or a claim for refund); avoiding conflicts of interest unless each affected client gives informed written consent; and not unreasonably delaying a matter before the IRS. A practitioner must also advise a client of any noncompliance, error, or omission and its consequences — but Circular 230 does not require the practitioner to notify the IRS of the client's error.

Circular 230 sanctions

The Office of Professional Responsibility (OPR) enforces Circular 230. For incompetence or disreputable conduct, willful violations, or recklessly giving false opinions, the Treasury may censure (a public reprimand), suspend, or disbar a practitioner from practice before the IRS, and may impose a monetary penalty up to the gross income derived from the offending conduct. Disbarment requires willful, reckless, or grossly incompetent conduct — not a mere good-faith mistake.

Preparer penalties under the Code

The Internal Revenue Code imposes its own penalties on paid preparers. §6694 targets understatements from unreasonable positions: a position lacking substantial authority (or, if disclosed, lacking a reasonable basis; for a tax shelter or reportable transaction the bar rises to more likely than not) triggers a penalty of the greater of $1,000 or 50% of the income the preparer derived from the return. If the understatement is willful or reckless, the penalty rises to the greater of $5,000 or 75% of that income. §6695 imposes smaller fixed penalties for procedural failures — failing to sign the return, failing to furnish the taxpayer a copy, failing to keep records, failing to provide a preparer tax identification number (PTIN), or negotiating a client's refund check. §6713 and §7216 penalize the unauthorized disclosure or use of taxpayer information, with §7216 carrying criminal exposure.

The reporting-standards ladder

Several confidence thresholds recur, and the exam tests their order. From lowest to highest: frivolous (not arguable); reasonable basis (roughly a 20%-or-greater chance of success — the minimum for a disclosed position); substantial authority (roughly 40%, the standard for an undisclosed position); more likely than not (greater than 50%, required for tax shelters and to avoid certain penalties); and, highest in practice, a should/will opinion. Adequate disclosure of a position is made on Form 8275 (or 8275-R for a position contrary to a regulation), which can reduce both preparer and taxpayer penalties when the position has a reasonable basis.

AICPA Statements on Standards for Tax Services

The SSTS are enforceable standards for AICPA members in tax practice. Their core rules: a member should not recommend a position unless it meets the applicable reporting standard, and should advise the client of potential penalties; a member may rely in good faith on client-provided information but should make reasonable inquiries when information appears incorrect, incomplete, or inconsistent; a member may use the taxpayer's estimates if reasonable under the circumstances and not presented as exact; on learning of an error in a previously filed return, the member should advise the client to correct it but may not notify the IRS without the client's consent (except where the law requires it); and advice should reflect professional competence and serve the client's needs. The SSTS parallel Circular 230 but are AICPA-enforced and apply specifically to members.

Taxpayer penalties

Separate from the preparer, the taxpayer faces penalties. The accuracy-related penalty (§6662) is 20% of the underpayment attributable to negligence, disregard of rules, or a substantial understatement (for an individual, generally more than the greater of 10% of the correct tax or $5,000). The civil fraud penalty (§6663) is 75% of the portion of the underpayment due to fraud. Failure to file (§6651) runs at 5% per month (up to 25%), while failure to pay runs at 0.5% per month; in a month when both apply, the failure-to-file penalty is reduced by the failure-to-pay amount. A reasonable-cause defense, shown by good-faith effort, can abate many of these — but never fraud.

Statutes of limitations and the audit path

The IRS generally must assess additional tax within three years of the later of the due date or the filing date. That extends to six years if the taxpayer omits more than 25% of gross income, and is unlimited for a false or fraudulent return or a failure to file. A taxpayer's refund claim must be filed within the later of three years from filing or two years from payment. A disputed examination goes first to IRS Appeals, an independent function that weighs the hazards of litigation; unresolved cases proceed to the U.S. Tax Court (no prepayment of the tax required), or to a U.S. District Court or the Court of Federal Claims after the taxpayer pays the tax and sues for a refund. These procedures, the penalty regime, and the practitioner standards together define the compliance environment in which every later REG topic is applied.

Bringing it to the construction client

For MBG these rules are concrete. If the CPA takes an aggressive position on the deductibility of a large equipment expenditure, the position needs substantial authority to go undisclosed, or a reasonable basis plus a Form 8275 disclosure, or the preparer risks the §6694 penalty. If Jordan Reed supplies an estimate of materials consumed on an in-progress job, the SSTS permit a reasonable estimate that is not held out as precise. And if the prior-year return overstated a deduction, the CPA must advise correction but cannot go behind the client to the IRS. The professional-responsibility layer is, in short, the frame around the tax computations the rest of REG teaches — get the duty and the standard right before you get the number right.

CMA bridge

CMA month 12 taught the IMA ethics standards for the internal management accountant; REG covers the tax practitioner's parallel but distinct duties under Circular 230 and the SSTS, plus the statutory penalties the IMA framework never reaches. Both demand integrity and a refusal to misrepresent — REG adds the federal enforcement teeth.

Practice and recap

  1. Know who has unlimited practice rights (attorneys, CPAs, EAs) and the core Circular 230 duties.
  2. Apply the §6694 preparer penalty (greater of $1,000/50%; willful or reckless, $5,000/75%).
  3. Order the standards: reasonable basis (disclosed) < substantial authority (undisclosed) < more likely than not (shelters).
  4. Distinguish the §6662 20% accuracy penalty from the §6663 75% fraud penalty, and know the 3/6/unlimited-year assessment statutes.

Recap: Circular 230 and the SSTS govern how a preparer must act; an undisclosed position needs substantial authority while a disclosed one needs reasonable basis (Form 8275); the §6694 preparer penalty is the greater of $1,000 or 50% of the fee; taxpayers face a 20% accuracy or 75% fraud penalty; and assessment is generally 3 years, 6 if more than 25% of gross income is omitted, and unlimited for fraud.

weeks.title: REG U1·W2 — Individual Taxation I: Gross Income, Exclusions & AGI (CPA Core)
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — building the individual return from the top down

The individual return is a waterfall: gross income minus adjustments gives adjusted gross income (AGI); AGI minus deductions gives taxable income; tax minus credits gives the liability. This week builds the top of that waterfall — what counts as income, what is excluded, and the above-the-line adjustments that produce AGI. Jordan Reed, the owner of MBG, reports the construction profit on a personal return, so these rules are not abstract for our case.

Filing status

Five statuses set the rate brackets and standard deduction: single; married filing jointly (MFJ); married filing separately (MFS); head of household (HOH) — an unmarried (or considered-unmarried) taxpayer who pays more than half the cost of maintaining a home for a qualifying person for more than half the year; and qualifying surviving spouse — available for two years after a spouse's death if the taxpayer maintains a home for a dependent child. Marital status is generally determined on the last day of the year. HOH is heavily tested because it offers better brackets and a larger standard deduction than single.

Gross income — the broad rule

§61 defines gross income as all income from whatever source derived unless a specific provision excludes it. Common inclusions: wages, interest, dividends, business income (Schedule C), capital gains, rents and royalties, unemployment compensation, gambling winnings, taxable state refunds (only if the tax was deducted and gave a benefit — the tax-benefit rule), and a portion of Social Security benefits for higher-income recipients. Qualified dividends and long-term capital gains are included in gross income but taxed at preferential rates (0/15/20%).

Timing and a TCJA trap

Most individuals are cash-basis: income is recognized when actually or constructively received (available without substantial restriction), and expenses when paid. A classic trap is alimony: for divorce or separation instruments executed after 2018, alimony is neither deductible by the payer nor income to the recipient (the TCJA reversed the old rule, which still governs pre-2019 agreements). Child support is never income to the recipient and never deductible. Prizes and awards are generally taxable at fair value.

Exclusions from gross income

Specific provisions remove items from income. Frequently tested exclusions: gifts and inheritances (excluded to the recipient — the donor may owe transfer tax); life insurance proceeds paid by reason of death; municipal bond interest (state/local government interest); qualified scholarships for tuition and required fees (but amounts for room and board are taxable); the §121 gain exclusion on a principal residence — up to $250,000 (single) / $500,000 (MFJ) if owned and used as the principal residence for two of the last five years; qualified employer fringe benefits (employer-paid health coverage, §132 no-additional-cost and de-minimis fringes); and damages for physical injury or sickness (but not punitive damages or most emotional-distress awards).

Business income and self-employment tax

An owner-operated trade or business reports on Schedule C: gross receipts minus ordinary and necessary business expenses equals net profit, which flows to the Form 1040 and into AGI. Net Schedule C profit also bears self-employment (SE) tax: 92.35% of net SE earnings is multiplied by 15.3% (12.4% Social Security up to the annual wage base, plus 2.9% Medicare with no cap, and an extra 0.9% Medicare surtax on high earners). The employer-equivalent half of the SE tax is an adjustment to income. For MBG's owner this is the bridge between the construction P&L and the personal return.

Adjustments to income (above the line)

Adjustments are subtracted from gross income to reach AGI and are available whether or not the taxpayer itemizes — hence valuable. The tested list includes: one-half of self-employment tax; the self-employed health insurance deduction; self-employed retirement contributions (SEP/SIMPLE); health savings account (HSA) contributions; traditional IRA contributions (subject to active-participant phaseouts); student loan interest (up to $2,500, phased out); and educator expenses. AGI matters because it is the reference point for many phaseouts, the medical-expense and charitable thresholds, and the taxability of Social Security.

Worked AGI on the construction owner

Illustrative: Jordan Reed's personal return shows Schedule C net profit of $120,000, taxable interest of $2,000, and qualified dividends of $3,000 — gross income of $125,000. Adjustments: net SE earnings = $120,000 × 0.9235 = $110,820; SE tax = $110,820 × 15.3% ≈ $16,955, so the one-half deduction is about $8,478; plus a self-employed health insurance deduction of $9,000. AGI = $125,000 − $8,478 − $9,000 = $107,522. The qualified dividends remain in that total but will be taxed at the preferential rate when the liability is computed next week.

Retirement distributions, Social Security, and debt forgiveness

Several income items carry their own rules. Traditional IRA and qualified-plan distributions are ordinary income, and a 10% penalty applies to withdrawals before age 59½ absent an exception, while qualified Roth distributions are entirely tax-free. Social Security benefits are taxed in tiers — as provisional income rises, up to 85% of benefits becomes taxable, and none is taxable for low-income recipients. Cancellation of indebtedness is generally income under §61, but it is excluded in bankruptcy and to the extent the taxpayer is insolvent; the separate qualified-principal-residence-debt exclusion applied only to discharges completed by the end of 2025 (or under a written agreement entered into by then) per IRS Publication 4681, and is not available for later discharges. A state tax refund is income only under the tax-benefit rule — taxable just to the extent the prior deduction produced a benefit, which the SALT cap can reduce.

Dependents and the kiddie tax

A dependent is a qualifying child or qualifying relative meeting the relationship, age, residency, support, and gross-income tests; dependents drive credits and filing thresholds even though the personal exemption is permanently set at zero (Public Law 119-21 §70103 made the post-2017 suspension permanent). A dependent's own standard deduction is limited — broadly the greater of a small floor or earned income plus a set amount, capped at the regular standard deduction. The kiddie tax then taxes a child's net unearned income above an annual threshold at the parents' marginal rate, preventing families from shifting investment income to a low-bracket child. Wages a child genuinely earns working for the construction business are earned income to the child and escape the kiddie tax — a legitimate, often-tested family planning point.

CMA bridge

CMA taught how MBG's construction profit is measured for the financial statements; REG shows how that same profit is taxed on the owner's personal return — Schedule C net profit, self-employment tax, and the adjustments that convert business income into the individual's AGI. The book-to-tax mindset from FAR's ASC 740 unit reappears here from the taxpayer's side.

Practice and recap

  1. Order the waterfall: gross income − adjustments = AGI; identify the five filing statuses (HOH is high-yield).
  2. Apply §61: income from all sources unless excluded; watch the post-2018 alimony reversal.
  3. Know the common exclusions — gifts/inheritances, life insurance, municipal interest, §121 home gain, qualified scholarships.
  4. Compute SE tax (92.35% × 15.3%) and deduct one-half; list the above-the-line adjustments.

Recap: gross income is everything not specifically excluded; key exclusions include gifts, life insurance, municipal interest, and the $250k/$500k §121 home-sale gain; one-half of self-employment tax and self-employed health insurance are above-the-line adjustments; and for MBG's owner a $125,000 gross income nets to an AGI of $107,522 after those adjustments — the figure that drives the deductions, the QBI deduction, and the credits computed next week.

weeks.title: REG U1·W3 — Individual Taxation II: Deductions, QBI, Credits & Computation (CPA Core)
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — from AGI to the check

Last week ended at AGI. This week finishes the individual return: subtract the greater of the standard or itemized deduction and the qualified business income (QBI) deduction to reach taxable income, apply the rate schedule (with preferential rates on qualified dividends and long-term gains), and subtract credits to reach the liability — then compare to payments. The QBI deduction in particular matters to MBG's owner, because a construction contractor is not a specified service business.

Standard versus itemized deductions

A taxpayer deducts the greater of the standard deduction (a fixed amount by filing status, larger for the age-65-or-blind) or itemized deductions on Schedule A. After the TCJA nearly doubled the standard deduction, most taxpayers take it, so the exam tests when itemizing wins.

Itemized deductions (Schedule A)

The main itemized categories: medical expenses to the extent they exceed 7.5% of AGI; state and local taxes (SALT) — income (or sales) plus property taxes — capped for 2026 at $40,400 ($40,000 for 2025), subject to a MAGI phasedown to a $10,000 floor for high earners and halved for MFS — Public Law 119-21 §70120; home mortgage interest on acquisition debt up to $750,000 (made permanent by Public Law 119-21; pre-2018 loans grandfathered at $1,000,000); investment interest limited to net investment income; charitable contributions — cash up to 60% of AGI, and appreciated long-term capital-gain property at fair market value up to 30% of AGI; and casualty and theft losses only if attributable to a federally declared disaster (and, for tax years after 2025, a qualifying state-declared disaster). Miscellaneous 2%-of-AGI itemized deductions are permanently terminated (Public Law 119-21 Section 70110), while the above-the-line educator-expense deduction remains.

The qualified business income deduction (§199A)

Owners of passthrough businesses (sole proprietorships, partnerships, S corporations) may deduct up to 20% of qualified business income — a deduction taken after AGI that does not reduce SE tax. The deduction is the lesser of (a) 20% of QBI or (b) 20% of taxable income minus net capital gain (net capital gain includes qualified dividends). Above taxable-income thresholds, two further limits apply: a W-2 wages / UBIA-of-property cap, and a phaseout for a specified service trade or business (SSTB) — law, accounting, health, consulting, and similar. Construction is not an SSTB, so MBG's owner keeps the deduction even above the threshold (subject only to the wage/property cap). Worked limit: if QBI is $100,000 and taxable income less net capital gain is $90,000, the deduction is the lesser of $20,000 (20% × QBI) or $18,000 (20% × $90,000) = $18,000 — the taxable-income limit binds.

Computing the tax

Ordinary taxable income runs through the progressive rate brackets for the filing status. But qualified dividends and net long-term capital gains are pulled out and taxed at the preferential 0% / 15% / 20% rates, stacked on top of ordinary income to determine which preferential rate applies. High earners also owe the 3.8% net investment income tax on the lesser of net investment income or the excess of modified AGI over a threshold. The result is the gross tax before credits.

Credits — nonrefundable and refundable

Credits reduce tax dollar-for-dollar and are more valuable than deductions. Nonrefundable credits can reduce the tax to zero but not below: the base child tax credit, the child and dependent care credit, the lifetime learning education credit, the foreign tax credit, and the retirement savings credit. Refundable credits can generate a refund beyond the tax owed: the earned income credit (EIC), the additional child tax credit, and the partly refundable American Opportunity Tax Credit (AOTC). Knowing which credits are refundable is a recurring exam point.

The alternative minimum tax

The AMT is a parallel system that limits the benefit of certain preferences. Start from regular taxable income, add back preference and adjustment items (the SALT deduction, certain depreciation, private-activity-bond interest, incentive-stock-option bargain elements), subtract the AMT exemption (phased out at higher income), and apply the 26%/28% AMT rates to alternative minimum taxable income. The taxpayer pays the greater of regular tax or the tentative minimum tax. Because the TCJA raised the exemption, far fewer individuals owe AMT now, but it remains testable.

Payments and the construction owner

The liability is settled by withholding (from wages) and quarterly estimated payments. A self-employed contractor like MBG's owner has no withholding, so estimates matter: to avoid an underpayment penalty the taxpayer generally must pay the lesser of 90% of the current-year tax or 100% of the prior-year tax (110% if prior-year AGI exceeded $150,000). Putting it together — deductions, the QBI deduction, the rate schedule, credits, and payments — converts the AGI from last week into the final number on the return, and completes the individual-tax arc of REG Unit 1.

Education and family credits in detail

The exam tests the contours of the common credits. The American Opportunity Tax Credit is up to $2,500 per student (100% of the first $2,000 of qualified expenses plus 25% of the next $2,000) for the first four years of postsecondary education, and is 40% refundable. The Lifetime Learning Credit is 20% of up to $10,000 of expenses (a $2,000 maximum) per return, nonrefundable, with no year limit. The child tax credit is a per-qualifying-child amount that phases out at higher AGI, with a refundable additional child tax credit portion. The child and dependent care credit is a percentage of up to $3,000 of care expenses for one dependent ($6,000 for two or more) incurred to enable the taxpayer to work. Each credit has its own AGI phaseout, which is why they are sequenced carefully on the return.

Additional taxes and the underpayment mechanics

Beyond the income tax and AMT, high earners face the 0.9% additional Medicare tax on wages and self-employment income above a threshold and the 3.8% net investment income tax on the lesser of net investment income or modified AGI over the threshold. The return reconciles the total tax to payments — withholding (treated as paid evenly through the year) plus quarterly estimates. If payments fall short of the safe harbor, the §6654 underpayment penalty accrues like interest on the shortfall for each quarter it persists. Because a contractor's income is lumpy, the annualized-income installment method can lower the required payment in slow quarters, matching estimates to when the construction cash actually arrives rather than assuming even income.

CMA bridge

CMA month 9 weighed decisions on a marginal, after-tax basis; REG supplies the actual individual-tax machinery behind that after-tax rate — the brackets, the preferential rates on capital gains, the QBI deduction, and the credits that determine an owner's true marginal cost of a dollar of construction profit.

Practice and recap

  1. Take the greater of the standard or itemized deduction; know the 2026 SALT cap ($40,400, phased down for high MAGI to a $10,000 floor), the 7.5%-of-AGI medical floor, and the $750,000 mortgage-acquisition limit.
  2. Apply §199A: 20% of QBI, limited to 20% of taxable income less net capital gain; construction is not an SSTB.
  3. Tax ordinary income at the brackets; tax qualified dividends and LTCG at 0/15/20%.
  4. Separate refundable credits (EIC, additional CTC, AOTC) from nonrefundable; pay estimates at 90%/100%/110% safe harbors.

Recap: taxable income is AGI minus the greater of standard or itemized deductions and minus the §199A QBI deduction (lesser of 20% of QBI or 20% of taxable income less net capital gain); ordinary income runs the brackets while qualified dividends and long-term gains get 0/15/20%; refundable credits like the EIC can exceed the tax; and a self-employed owner avoids penalty by meeting the 90%/100%/110% estimated-tax safe harbor.
