weeks.title: REG U1·W4 — Property Transactions: Basis, Capital vs Ordinary, §1231/1245/1250 & §1031 (CPA Core)
weeks.lessonHtml:
Cold open — every disposition is one subtraction

When MBG sells a backhoe or a parcel of land, the tax answer starts with one formula: gain or loss = amount realized − adjusted basis. The hard part is then characterizing the result — capital or ordinary, and at what rate — because depreciation recapture and the §1231 rules can split a single sale into pieces. This week covers basis, the capital/ordinary divide, recapture, and the like-kind deferral that lets a contractor roll real estate forward.

Basis — cost, adjusted, gift, and inheritance

Cost basis is what you paid, including acquisition costs. Adjusted basis = cost + capital improvements − depreciation/cost recovery taken. Two special rules recur. Gifted property: the donee takes the donor's carryover basis for computing a gain; for a loss, basis is the lesser of carryover basis or fair market value at the gift date (the dual-basis rule, which can produce no gain and no loss in the middle range); the donor's holding period tacks on only when the carryover (gain) basis is used — if the FMV loss basis applies, the holding period instead begins on the gift date. Inherited property takes a stepped-up (or down) basis equal to FMV at the date of death, and is automatically long-term regardless of how long the heir holds it.

Capital assets, netting, and the loss limit

A capital asset is defined by exclusion: §1221 says everything is capital except inventory, accounts receivable, depreciable business property, and real property used in a trade or business. Long-term means held more than one year. Individuals net short-term and long-term gains and losses; a net capital loss is deductible against ordinary income only up to $3,000 per year, with the excess carried forward indefinitely. Net long-term gains enjoy the preferential 0/15/20% rates from last week.

§1231 — the best of both worlds

Depreciable property and real property used in a business and held more than one year are §1231 assets. Their magic: a net §1231 gain for the year is treated as long-term capital gain (preferential rates), while a net §1231 loss is ordinary (fully deductible against other income). A five-year lookback prevents abuse — current-year §1231 gain is recharacterized as ordinary to the extent of net §1231 losses deducted in the prior five years.

Depreciation recapture — §1245 and §1250

Before §1231 applies, recapture converts part of the gain to ordinary income. §1245 (depreciable personal property — equipment, vehicles): gain is ordinary income to the extent of depreciation taken; only the excess is §1231 gain. Worked example: MBG sells a loader that cost $100,000 with $60,000 accumulated depreciation (adjusted basis $40,000). Sold for $70,000, the $30,000 gain is entirely ordinary recapture (it is within the $60,000 of depreciation). Sold instead for $110,000, the $70,000 gain is $60,000 ordinary recapture plus $10,000 §1231 gain (long-term). §1250 (depreciable real property): with straight-line depreciation there is generally no ordinary recapture, but the straight-line depreciation is unrecaptured §1250 gain — the lesser of the depreciation taken or the recognized §1231 gain — taxed at a maximum 25% rate.

§1031 like-kind exchanges

A like-kind exchange defers gain when business or investment property is swapped for like-kind property. Post-TCJA, §1031 applies only to real property (equipment no longer qualifies). No gain is recognized except to the extent of boot (cash or non-like-kind property received); recognized gain = the lesser of realized gain or boot. The deferred gain is preserved in a substituted basis. Worked example: MBG exchanges land with a $200,000 adjusted basis for like-kind land worth $260,000 and receives no boot — no gain is recognized, the new land takes a $200,000 carryover basis, and the $60,000 gain is deferred until a future taxable sale. Receiving $20,000 of cash boot would force recognition of $20,000 of the gain.

Cost recovery — MACRS, §179, and bonus

The depreciation that drives recapture comes from MACRS: personal property uses the 200%-declining-balance method over 5- or 7-year lives with a half-year (or mid-quarter) convention; real property uses straight-line over 27.5 years (residential) or 39 years (nonresidential). Two accelerators matter for a contractor: §179 expensing lets a business immediately deduct the cost of qualifying property up to an annual limit, phased out as purchases get large and capped at business taxable income; and bonus depreciation allows an additional first-year percentage on qualifying new or used property. Both increase current deductions — and the depreciation that §1245 will later recapture.

Loss limitations — wash sales and related parties

Two anti-abuse rules disallow losses. The wash-sale rule disallows a loss on a security sold and repurchased within 30 days before or after; the disallowed loss is added to the basis of the replacement. §267 disallows a loss on a sale to a related party (family members, a more-than-50%-owned entity); the related buyer may later use the disallowed loss to offset a gain on resale. These rules, with recapture and §1231, complete the property-transaction toolkit — and round out REG Unit 1.

Installment sales and involuntary conversions

Two more deferral rules round out dispositions. The installment method spreads gain on a sale with payments received over more than one year: each payment recognizes gain equal to the payment times the gross-profit percentage (gross profit ÷ contract price). It is not available for inventory or for the depreciation-recapture portion, which is fully taxed in the year of sale even if no cash is yet received. An involuntary conversion (§1033) — property destroyed, stolen, or condemned — lets the taxpayer defer gain by reinvesting the proceeds in qualified replacement property within the statutory window (generally two years, three for condemned business real property); gain is recognized only to the extent the proceeds are not reinvested. Both rules, like §1031, defer rather than erase gain and carry the basis and deferred gain forward.

Holding period and the netting order

Character also turns on the holding period: more than one year is long-term, one year or less is short-term, and the period generally starts the day after acquisition. For gifted property the period tacks the donor's, and inherited property is automatically long-term. In capital netting, short-term gains and losses net together and long-term gains and losses net together; a net short-term gain is taxed at ordinary rates while a net long-term gain gets the preferential rate. A net loss in one class then offsets net gain in the other before the $3,000 ordinary-offset limit applies. Getting the holding period and this netting order right is exactly what fixes the rate on MBG's equipment and land sales.

CMA bridge

CMA capital budgeting (month 11) used the depreciation tax shield and after-tax salvage value as cash flows; REG supplies the rules behind them — MACRS and §179 create the shield, and §1245/§1250 recapture determines how the salvage proceeds are taxed when the asset is finally sold. The book gain/loss from FAR becomes a characterized tax gain here.

Practice and recap

  1. Compute gain/loss as amount realized minus adjusted basis; know gift carryover/dual basis and the inherited FMV step-up (auto-long-term).
  2. Net capital gains/losses; cap an individual's net capital loss at $3,000 against ordinary income.
  3. Apply §1231 (net gain = LTCG, net loss = ordinary) after §1245/§1250 recapture.
  4. Defer gain under §1031 (real property only) except to the extent of boot; carry over basis.

Recap: characterization is everything — §1231 net gains become long-term capital gain while net losses are ordinary, §1245 recaptures depreciation as ordinary up to the gain (so MBG's $30,000 loader gain is all ordinary but a $70,000 gain splits $60k ordinary / $10k §1231), real-property straight-line depreciation is unrecaptured §1250 gain (the lesser of depreciation taken or recognized gain) at a 25% max, and §1031 defers real-property gain except to the extent of boot with a carryover basis.
